lessons.title: Types of signals

scenes.text: An ECG trace is a continuous-time signal; a thermometer logging every minute gives a discrete-time sequence.
Classifying signals tells us which tools apply.

steps.title: Classifications
steps.body:
- CT x(t) vs DT x[n]; analog vs digital (amplitude quantised).
- **Even** x(−t) = x(t); **odd** x(−t) = −x(t). Any signal = xₑ + xₒ with xₑ = [x(t) + x(−t)]/2, xₒ = [x(t) − x(−t)]/2.
- **Periodic:** x(t + T) = x(t). Sum of periodic signals is periodic if the ratio of periods is rational; fundamental period = LCM.
- DT sinusoid cos(Ω₀n) is periodic only if Ω₀/2π is rational: N = 2πm/Ω₀ (smallest integer).

steps.title: Energy and power
steps.body:
E = ∫|x(t)|²dt (Σ|x[n]|² for DT). P = lim (1/2T)∫₋ᵀᵀ|x|²dt.
Energy signal: 0 < E < ∞ (P = 0) — e.g. finite pulses, decaying exponentials. Power signal: 0 < P < ∞ (E = ∞) — periodic signals, step. A signal can be neither (e.g. t·u(t)).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** x(t) = cos 4t + sin 6t: T₁ = π/2, T₂ = π/3 ⇒ T = π.

**Example 2.** x[n] = cos(πn/4): N = 8. x[n] = cos(n/4): Ω₀/2π = 1/(8π) irrational ⇒ not periodic.

**Example 3.** x(t) = e^(−2t)u(t): E = ∫₀^∞ e^(−4t)dt = 1/4 ⇒ energy signal.

**Example 4.** x(t) = 5 cos(10t): P = 25/2 = 12.5 ⇒ power signal.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming every DT sinusoid is periodic.
- Using amplitude instead of amplitude² for power (A²/2 for a sinusoid).
- Calling the step an energy signal (E is infinite).

quiz.why: sin 3t has period 2π/3 and cos 2t has period π. The smallest common multiple is 2π (3 and 2 periods).
The even part of x(t) is [x(t) + x(−t)]/2. The odd part is [x(t) − x(−t)]/2.
The power of A cos ωt is A²/2. For A = 3, that is 9/2 = 4.5.
For DT, N = 2πm/Ω₀ must be an integer. With Ω₀ = 0.3π, N = 2m/0.3 = 20m/3, so the smallest integer is for m = 3: N = 20.

quiz.q: Energy of a unit-height pulse of width 2
quiz.why: Energy = ∫|x(t)|² dt = 1² × 2 = 2.

lessons.title: Elementary signals

scenes.text: A switch closing at t = 0 is a step; a hammer tap on a structure is (almost) an impulse.
Complicated signals are built from these simple blocks.

steps.title: Definitions and relations
steps.body:
- Unit step u(t) = 1 for t ≥ 0, 0 for t < 0.
- Unit impulse δ(t): zero for t ≠ 0, ∫δ dt = 1. δ(t) = du/dt; u(t) = ∫₋∞ᵗ δ(τ)dτ.
- Ramp r(t) = t·u(t); dr/dt = u(t).
- **Sifting:** ∫x(t)δ(t − t₀)dt = x(t₀); x(t)δ(t − t₀) = x(t₀)δ(t − t₀).
- Scaling: δ(at) = δ(t)/|a|.
- DT: δ[n] = u[n] − u[n − 1]; u[n] = Σ_(k≤n) δ[k].
- Complex exponential e^(st), s = σ + jω: grows/decays with σ, oscillates with ω.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** ∫₋∞^∞ (t² + 3)δ(t − 2)dt = 7.

**Example 2.** ∫₋∞^∞ e^(−t)δ(2t − 4)dt = ½e^(−2) (since δ(2t − 4) = ½δ(t − 2)).

**Example 3.** A rectangular pulse of height 3 from t = 1 to 4: x(t) = 3[u(t − 1) − u(t − 4)].

**Example 4.** Triangle rising from 0 at t = 0 to 1 at t = 1 then falling to 0 at t = 2: x = r(t) − 2r(t − 1) + r(t − 2).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the 1/|a| in δ(at).
- Sifting when the impulse lies outside the integration limits (result is 0).
- Writing pulses as u(t − a) + u(t − b) instead of a difference.

quiz.why: The derivative of the unit step is the unit impulse, du/dt = δ(t).
By the sifting property, ∫x(t)δ(t − 5)dt = x(5).
δ(at) = δ(t)/|a|. So δ(3t) = δ(t)/3.
u(t) − u(t − 3) is 1 from 0 to 3. Multiplying by 2 gives a pulse of height 2.
δ[n] = u[n] − u[n − 1], the first difference of the unit step.

lessons.title: Operations on signals

scenes.text: A DJ reverses a clip, then plays it at double speed starting 2 s later.
Order matters: shift, scale and reverse must be applied carefully.

steps.title: Operations
steps.body:
- Time shift x(t − t₀): delay (right) if t₀ > 0.
- Time scaling x(at): compress if |a| > 1, expand if |a| < 1.
- Reversal x(−t): mirror about t = 0.
- y(t) = x(at + b): method 1 — shift first by b to get x(t + b), then scale by a; method 2 — write x(a(t + b/a)): scale then shift by b/a.
DT scaling x[2n] keeps every second sample (decimation) — information can be lost.

steps.title: Quick check
steps.body: To find where y(t) = x(at + b) lives, solve 'argument within the original support' — inequalities never get the order wrong.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Shifting by b after scaling (should shift by b/a).
- Reversing the direction of a delay.
- Forgetting that inequalities flip when dividing by a negative a.

quiz.q: Support of x(2t) if x lives on [0, 4]
quiz.why: x(2t) is x compressed by 2. A signal on [0, 4] now lives on [0, 2].
x(−t + 2) is non-zero when 0 ≤ 2 − t ≤ 2, i.e. 0 ≤ t ≤ 2. So it lives on [0, 2] (a reversed and shifted copy).
x[3n] picks every 3rd sample of x[n]. That is decimation by 3.

lessons.title: System properties

scenes.text: An audio amplifier distorts when overdriven — it stops being linear.
We test system properties with simple input–output reasoning.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Linear:** superposition — T{ax₁ + bx₂} = aT{x₁} + bT{x₂} (implies zero input → zero output).
- **Time-invariant:** shifting the input shifts the output by the same amount.
- **Causal:** output depends only on present/past inputs.
- **Memoryless (static):** output depends only on the present input.
- **BIBO stable:** every bounded input gives a bounded output.
- **Invertible:** distinct inputs give distinct outputs.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** y(t) = t·x(t): linear ✔; time-variant (coefficient t) ✘; causal ✔; memoryless ✔; unstable (x = 1 gives y = t, unbounded).

**Example 2.** y(t) = x(t) + 2: non-linear (zero input gives 2); TI ✔; causal ✔.

**Example 3.** y[n] = x[n + 1]: linear, TI, **non-causal** (future input).

**Example 4.** y(t) = x(2t): linear, time-variant, non-causal (y(1) needs x(2)).

**Example 5.** y(t) = ∫₋∞ᵗ x(τ)dτ: linear, TI, causal, with memory, unstable (u(t) → ramp).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling y = x + 2 linear (it is affine).
- Testing time-invariance by shifting only the input inside but forgetting to shift t elsewhere.
- Assuming time scaling is time-invariant.

quiz.why: Linear systems satisfy superposition: the response to a sum of inputs is the sum of the responses, and scaling carries through.
y[n] = x[n + 2] uses a future input sample, so the system is non-causal.
y(t) = 3x(t) multiplies by a constant gain. It depends only on the present input, and is linear and time-invariant.
An integrator turns a bounded step input into a ramp, which grows without bound. So it is not BIBO stable.
For y(t) = x(t) + 5, a zero input gives output 5, not 0. A linear system must give zero output for zero input, so it is not linear.

lessons.title: Impulse response and the convolution sum

scenes.text: Clap once in a hall and record the echoes — that is its impulse response.
Any music played there = convolution of the music with that response.

steps.title: Convolution sum
steps.body:
Any x[n] = Σ x[k]δ[n − k]. For an LTI system with impulse response h[n]: y[n] = Σₖ x[k]h[n − k] = x[n] * h[n].
Length: if x has N₁ samples and h has N₂, y has N₁ + N₂ − 1 samples.

steps.title: Table (multiplication) method
steps.body: Write x across the top and h down the side, fill products, and sum along anti-diagonals — fast for short sequences.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Wrong start index of y (start = start(x) + start(h)).
- Forgetting to flip h when using the graphical method.
- Length errors (N₁ + N₂ − 1).

activity.prompt: Compute the convolution of x = [1, 2, 1] and h = [1, -1] without numpy and print the result list.
activity.starter:
x = [1, 2, 1]
h = [1, -1]
y = [0] * (len(x) + len(h) - 1)
# fill y[n] = sum x[k]*h[n-k]

print(y)
activity.solution:
x = [1, 2, 1]
h = [1, -1]
y = [0] * (len(x) + len(h) - 1)
for i in range(len(x)):
    for j in range(len(h)):
        y[i + j] += x[i] * h[j]
print(y)
activity.hint: Nested loops: add x[i]*h[j] into y[i+j].

quiz.q: Output length for x of 4 samples and h of 3
quiz.why: The convolution of lengths 4 and 3 has length 4 + 3 − 1 = 6.
Convolving with a shifted impulse shifts the signal: x[n] * δ[n − 2] = x[n − 2].
The impulse response completely describes an LTI system, since the output is the input convolved with it. This does not hold for non-LTI systems.
Convolve {1, 1} with {1, 1}: terms are 1, 1 + 1 = 2, 1. So {1, 2, 1}.

quiz.q: y[0] for x = {2, 3}, h = {4, 5} (both start at 0)
quiz.why: y[0] = x[0]h[0] = 2 × 4 = 8, since both signals start at 0.

lessons.title: Convolution integral

scenes.text: An RC low-pass filter has h(t) = (1/RC)e^(−t/RC)u(t).
Its response to any input is the convolution integral.

steps.title: Definition and graphical method
steps.body: y(t) = ∫₋∞^∞ x(τ)h(t − τ)dτ. Steps: flip h(τ) → h(−τ); shift by t; multiply by x(τ); integrate the overlap; repeat over ranges of t.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** x = u(t), h = e^(−at)u(t): y = ∫₀ᵗ e^(−a(t − τ))dτ = (1 − e^(−at))/a for t ≥ 0.

**Example 2.** Two unit pulses on [0, 1]: y(t) = triangle — t for 0 ≤ t ≤ 1, 2 − t for 1 ≤ t ≤ 2, 0 elsewhere.

**Example 3.** e^(−t)u(t) * e^(−2t)u(t) = (e^(−t) − e^(−2t))u(t).

steps.title: Useful results
steps.body:
- x(t) * δ(t − t₀) = x(t − t₀)
- x(t) * u(t) = ∫₋∞ᵗ x(τ)dτ
- Width of x * h = sum of widths; start = sum of starts.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Wrong integration limits for each interval of t.
- Forgetting u(t) on the final answer.
- Flipping x instead of h then mixing variables.

activity.prompt: y = u(t) * e^(−2t)u(t). Value of y(t) as t → ∞?

quiz.q: Convolution of two rectangles of equal width gives
quiz.why: Convolving two equal rectangles gives a triangle: the overlap area grows then shrinks linearly.
Convolving with δ(t) leaves the signal unchanged, since δ is the identity: x(t) * δ(t) = x(t).
Convolving with the unit step integrates the signal up to the present time: a running integral.

quiz.q: Width of a 2 s pulse convolved with a 3 s pulse
quiz.why: The width of the convolution of two finite pulses is the sum of the widths: 2 + 3 = 5 s.
In the Laplace domain, 1/(s + 1) squared is 1/(s + 1)², whose inverse is t e^(−t)u(t). Repeated poles give a factor of t.

lessons.title: Properties, causality and stability

scenes.text: Two equaliser stages in series act like one filter.
Associativity: h_total = h₁ * h₂ — and order doesn't matter.

steps.title: Properties
steps.body:
- Commutative x * h = h * x
- Associative (x * h₁) * h₂ = x * (h₁ * h₂) ⇒ cascade h = h₁ * h₂
- Distributive x * (h₁ + h₂) ⇒ parallel h = h₁ + h₂
- Causal LTI ⇔ h(t) = 0 for t < 0 (h[n] = 0 for n < 0)
- BIBO stable ⇔ ∫|h(t)|dt < ∞ (Σ|h[n]| < ∞)
- Memoryless ⇔ h = kδ

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** h[n] = (0.5)ⁿu[n]: Σ|h| = 2 < ∞ ⇒ stable; causal.

**Example 2.** h(t) = e^(2t)u(t): ∫ diverges ⇒ unstable.

**Example 3.** h[n] = u[n + 3] − u[n − 2]: non-zero for n = −3…1 ⇒ non-causal, stable (finite sum = 5).

**Example 4.** Cascade h₁ = δ[n] − δ[n − 1] with h₂ = u[n]: h = δ[n] (they undo each other — difference and accumulator are inverses).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Judging stability by h being bounded (need absolute integrability).
- Thinking cascade order matters for LTI systems.
- Forgetting that h(t) = u(t) is unstable.

quiz.why: A causal system cannot respond before the input, so its impulse response must be zero for t < 0.
An LTI system is BIBO stable if and only if its impulse response is absolutely integrable, ∫|h| < ∞.
In a parallel connection, the outputs add, so the overall impulse response is h₁ + h₂.
Σ|h[n]| = Σ (1/3)ⁿ for n ≥ 0 = 1/(1 − 1/3) = 3/2 = 1.5. The sum is finite, so the system is BIBO stable.
A memoryless LTI system output depends only on the present input, so h(t) = kδ(t) for a constant gain k.

lessons.title: Differential and difference equations

scenes.text: Stock analysts smooth prices with a 3-day moving average.
That is a difference equation: y[n] = (x[n] + x[n − 1] + x[n − 2])/3.

steps.title: LTI descriptions
steps.body:
CT: Σ aₖ dᵏy/dtᵏ = Σ bₖ dᵏx/dtᵏ; DT: Σ aₖ y[n − k] = Σ bₖ x[n − k] (with initial rest ⇒ LTI and causal).
- **FIR:** depends only on inputs (finite h). **IIR:** feedback from past outputs (infinite h).
Impulse response of y[n] − ay[n − 1] = x[n]: h[n] = aⁿu[n]. Of y′ + ay = x: h(t) = e^(−at)u(t).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** y[n] = 0.5y[n − 1] + x[n], x = δ[n], y[−1] = 0: y[0] = 1, y[1] = 0.5, y[2] = 0.25 … h[n] = (0.5)ⁿu[n].

**Example 2.** 3-point moving average h = {1/3, 1/3, 1/3} (FIR). Step response settles to 1 after 3 samples.

**Example 3.** Natural + forced response: y′ + 2y = 4u(t), y(0) = 0 ⇒ y = 2(1 − e^(−2t)).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting initial rest when claiming LTI.
- Calling a recursive equation FIR.
- Wrong sign of the feedback coefficient when iterating.

lessons.title: Continuous-time Fourier series

scenes.text: A spectrum analyser shows a square wave's spikes at f₀, 3f₀, 5f₀…
Those spikes are its Fourier series coefficients.

steps.title: Exponential form
steps.body:
x(t) = Σ cₖ e^(jkω₀t), ω₀ = 2π/T, cₖ = (1/T)∫_T x(t)e^(−jkω₀t)dt. For real x: c₋ₖ = cₖ*.
Trigonometric: a₀ + Σ(aₖ cos kω₀t + bₖ sin kω₀t) with aₖ = 2Re cₖ, bₖ = −2Im cₖ, a₀ = c₀ (average value).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** x(t) = cos ω₀t: c₁ = c₋₁ = ½, others 0.

**Example 2.** x(t) = 1 + sin(2ω₀t): c₀ = 1, c₂ = 1/(2j), c₋₂ = −1/(2j).

**Example 3.** Periodic rectangular pulse train, height A, width τ, period T: cₖ = (Aτ/T) sinc(kτ/T) where sinc(x) = sin(πx)/(πx). For 50% duty cycle, even harmonics vanish.

steps.title: Properties and power
steps.body: Time shift: x(t − t₀) ↔ cₖe^(−jkω₀t₀). Parseval: P = (1/T)∫|x|² = Σ|cₖ|². Even real x ⇒ real cₖ; odd real x ⇒ imaginary cₖ.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting 1/T in cₖ.
- Mixing the sinc conventions (sin x/x vs sin πx/πx).
- Counting only positive k in Parseval for complex coefficients.

quiz.why: c₀ is the k = 0 coefficient: the average (DC) value of the signal.

lessons.title: Fourier transform and standard pairs

scenes.text: A radar sends one short pulse, not a repeating wave.
For aperiodic signals the line spectrum becomes a continuous spectrum: the Fourier transform.

steps.title: Definition and pairs
steps.body:
X(jω) = ∫x(t)e^(−jωt)dt; x(t) = (1/2π)∫X(jω)e^(jωt)dω.
- δ(t) ↔ 1
- 1 ↔ 2πδ(ω)
- e^(−at)u(t) ↔ 1/(a + jω), a > 0

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** x = e^(−3t)u(t): X = 1/(3 + jω); |X| = 1/√(9 + ω²); ∠X = −tan⁻¹(ω/3).

**Example 2.** Pulse of height 1, width 2 centred at 0: X = 2 sin ω/ω; first zeros at ω = ±π.

**Example 3.** x = e^(−2|t|): X = 4/(4 + ω²).

steps.title: Time–bandwidth trade-off
steps.body: Narrower pulses have wider spectra — the first zero of a width-τ pulse is at f = 1/τ. That is why short pulses need wide bandwidth.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting a > 0 for e^(−at)u(t) to have a transform.
- Omitting the 2π factors between ω and f conventions.
- Writing the transform of a constant as 1 instead of 2πδ(ω).

quiz.why: The Fourier transform of δ(t) is 1, by the sifting property.
The transform of e^(−at)u(t) is 1/(a + jω), for a > 0.
A constant has all its energy at ω = 0. Its transform is an impulse, 2πδ(ω).

quiz.why: A pulse of width τ has its first spectral zero at f = 1/τ. For τ = 1 ms, that is 1 kHz.

lessons.title: Properties of the Fourier transform and Parseval

scenes.text: Multiplying a voice signal by a carrier shifts its spectrum up to the carrier frequency.
That is the modulation (frequency-shift) property.

steps.title: Properties
steps.body:
- Linearity
- Time shift x(t − t₀) ↔ e^(−jωt₀)X(jω) (magnitude unchanged)
- Frequency shift e^(jω₀t)x(t) ↔ X(j(ω − ω₀)); modulation x cos ω₀t ↔ ½[X(ω − ω₀) + X(ω + ω₀)]
- Scaling x(at) ↔ (1/|a|)X(jω/a)
- Differentiation dx/dt ↔ jωX; integration ↔ X/(jω) + πX(0)δ(ω)
- Convolution x * h ↔ XH; multiplication xy ↔ (1/2π)X * Y
- Duality; conjugate symmetry for real x: |X| even, ∠X odd
- **Parseval:** ∫|x|²dt = (1/2π)∫|X|²dω

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** FT of e^(−2(t − 1))u(t − 1) = e^(−jω)/(2 + jω).

**Example 2.** FT of t e^(−at)u(t) = 1/(a + jω)² (differentiation in frequency).

**Example 3.** Energy of e^(−t)u(t): time domain ∫e^(−2t) = 1/2; frequency: (1/2π)∫dω/(1 + ω²) = (1/2π)π = 1/2 ✔

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Changing |X| when a signal is only delayed.
- Missing the 1/|a| factor in scaling.
- Forgetting the 1/2π in Parseval (ω convention).

quiz.why: Multiplying by cos ω₀t shifts the spectrum to ±ω₀, each copy with half the amplitude.

lessons.title: Frequency response and the DTFT

scenes.text: Turning the bass knob changes how much each low frequency is passed.
An LTI system multiplies each frequency by H(jω).

steps.title: Frequency response
steps.body:
For LTI systems: y = x * h ⇒ Y = HX, H(jω) = FT of h. A sinusoid e^(jω₀t) in gives H(jω₀)e^(jω₀t) out — eigenfunction property. |H| = gain, ∠H = phase shift.
First-order low-pass RC: H = 1/(1 + jωRC); cut-off ω_c = 1/RC where |H| = 1/√2 (−3 dB). Ideal filters (LPF, HPF, BPF) are non-causal; practical filters approximate them.

steps.title: DTFT
steps.body:
X(e^(jΩ)) = Σ x[n]e^(−jΩn) — periodic in Ω with period 2π. Inverse: x[n] = (1/2π)∫_(2π) X e^(jΩn)dΩ.
- aⁿu[n] ↔ 1/(1 − ae^(−jΩ)), |a| < 1
- δ[n] ↔ 1
- Low frequencies near Ω = 0, highest near Ω = π.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** RC LPF with R = 1 kΩ, C = 1 µF: ω_c = 1000 rad/s (159 Hz). Input cos(1000t) ⇒ output (1/√2)cos(1000t − 45°).

**Example 2.** 2-point average h = {½, ½}: H(e^(jΩ)) = ½(1 + e^(−jΩ)) = e^(−jΩ/2)cos(Ω/2): passes Ω = 0 fully, blocks Ω = π (low-pass).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Expecting the DTFT to be aperiodic.
- Forgetting the phase shift in sinusoidal steady state.
- Calling ideal brick-wall filters realisable.

quiz.why: Complex exponentials e^(jωt) are eigenfunctions of LTI systems: the output is the same exponential times a constant, H(jω).
At the cut-off frequency, a first-order low-pass filter's gain is 1/√2, i.e. −3 dB.
The DTFT is periodic with period 2π, since e^(−jΩn) repeats when Ω increases by 2π.
The highest frequency in discrete time is Ω = π, where the sequence alternates sign every sample.
An ideal low-pass filter has a sinc impulse response, which starts before t = 0. So it is non-causal and cannot be built.

lessons.title: Laplace transform and ROC

scenes.text: A growing signal like eᵗu(t) has no Fourier transform.
Laplace adds a decay factor e^(−σt): X(s) exists in a region of the s-plane — the ROC.

steps.title: Definition and ROC
steps.body:
X(s) = ∫x(t)e^(−st)dt, s = σ + jω. ROC = values of s where the integral converges.
- Right-sided signals: ROC is right of the rightmost pole.
- Left-sided: left of the leftmost pole.
- Two-sided: a strip.
- ROC never contains poles.
- e^(−at)u(t) ↔ 1/(s + a), Re s > −a; −e^(−at)u(−t) ↔ 1/(s + a), Re s < −a (same expression, different ROC!).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** x = e^(−2t)u(t) + e^(−3t)u(t): X = 1/(s + 2) + 1/(s + 3), ROC Re s > −2.

**Example 2.** x = e^(−2t)u(t) + e^(3t)u(−t): X = 1/(s + 2) − 1/(s − 3), ROC −2 < Re s < 3.

**Example 3.** Inverse of 1/((s + 1)(s + 2)) with ROC Re s > −1: e^(−t) − e^(−2t) for t ≥ 0.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Giving X(s) without its ROC (the inverse is not unique).
- ROC including a pole.
- Treating the unilateral and bilateral transforms as identical for two-sided signals.

quiz.why: e^(−5t)u(t) is right-sided, and its transform 1/(s + 5) converges for Re s > −5.
The ROC cannot contain poles, because X(s) is infinite there.
The Laplace transform of δ(t) is 1, for all s, by the sifting property.

quiz.q: Same X(s) with different ROC gives
quiz.why: The same X(s) with different ROCs belongs to different time signals (right- or left-sided). So the ROC is needed for uniqueness.
The Laplace transform of u(t) is 1/s with ROC Re s > 0.

lessons.title: Transfer functions, poles, zeros and stability

scenes.text: A drone's controller has a transfer function H(s).
Poles in the right half-plane mean growing oscillations — instability.

steps.title: Transfer function
steps.body:
H(s) = Y(s)/X(s) = L{h(t)}. From a differential equation with zero ICs: Σaₖsᵏ Y = Σbₖsᵏ X. Poles = roots of the denominator, zeros = roots of the numerator.
**Causal & stable** LTI: ROC right of rightmost pole and includes the jω-axis ⇒ all poles in the left half-plane (Re p < 0).
Frequency response H(jω) = H(s) on the jω-axis (if the axis is in the ROC).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** y″ + 3y′ + 2y = x: H = 1/(s² + 3s + 2), poles −1, −2 ⇒ causal stable; h = (e^(−t) − e^(−2t))u(t).

**Example 2.** H = (s + 1)/(s² − s − 6) = (s + 1)/((s − 3)(s + 2)): pole at +3 ⇒ a causal version is unstable; a stable version (ROC −2 < Re s < 3) is non-causal.

**Example 3.** Second-order H = ω_n²/(s² + 2ζω_ns + ω_n²): underdamped ζ < 1 (complex poles), critically damped ζ = 1, overdamped ζ > 1.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling a system unstable just because it has a zero in the RHP (zeros don't affect stability).
- Forgetting that poles on the jω-axis give marginal (BIBO unstable) systems.
- Using initial conditions in transfer-function derivations (TF assumes zero ICs).

quiz.q: Causal LTI system is stable if all poles have
quiz.why: A causal LTI system is stable if all poles lie in the left half-plane, i.e. have negative real parts.
s² + 4 = 0 gives s² = −4, so s = ±2j.
Taking the Laplace transform of y′ + 5y = x gives (s + 5)Y = X, so H(s) = 1/(s + 5).

quiz.q: Zeros in the right half-plane affect
quiz.why: A zero in the right half-plane does not affect stability, which depends on the poles. It changes the phase and shape of the response (non-minimum phase).
ζ = 1 gives repeated real poles. That is critically damped.

lessons.title: Z-transform and inverse Z-transform

scenes.text: A DSP chip runs y[n] = x[n] + 0.9y[n − 1] millions of times a second.
The Z-transform turns that recursion into H(z) = 1/(1 − 0.9z⁻¹).

steps.title: Definition, pairs, ROC
steps.body:
X(z) = Σ x[n]z^(−n). ROC: annulus in the z-plane.
- δ[n] ↔ 1 (all z)
- aⁿu[n] ↔ 1/(1 − az⁻¹), |z| > |a|
- −aⁿu[−n − 1] ↔ 1/(1 − az⁻¹), |z| < |a|
- naⁿu[n] ↔ az⁻¹/(1 − az⁻¹)²
Properties: shift x[n − k] ↔ z^(−k)X(z); convolution ↔ product.
Causal & stable DT LTI ⇔ all poles inside the unit circle (ROC |z| > r_max includes |z| = 1).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting that the ROC decides the inverse.
- Doing partial fractions in z instead of z⁻¹ inconsistently.
- Stability test using the left half-plane (for DT it's the unit circle).

activity.text: aⁿu[n] ↔ 1/(1 − a z^___) with ROC |z| > |a|; a causal DT system is stable if all poles lie inside the unit ___.

quiz.why: A delay of 3 samples multiplies the Z-transform by z⁻³, so δ[n − 3] has transform z⁻³.
(0.8)ⁿu[n] is right-sided, so its ROC is outside the pole: |z| > 0.8.
A causal DT system is stable when all poles lie inside the unit circle, so the ROC includes it.
For the FIR {1, 1}, H(z) = 1 + z⁻¹.
Convolution in time becomes multiplication of Z-transforms.

lessons.title: Sampling theorem, aliasing and reconstruction

scenes.text: In films, fast-spinning wheels can seem to rotate backwards.
The camera samples too slowly — that is aliasing.

steps.title: Sampling theorem
steps.body:
A band-limited signal with maximum frequency f_m is uniquely recovered from samples taken at f_s > 2f_m (Nyquist rate = 2f_m). Ideal sampling multiplies by an impulse train; the spectrum repeats every f_s.
Reconstruction: ideal low-pass filter (cut-off f_s/2) ⇒ sinc interpolation. Practical systems use an anti-aliasing filter before sampling and oversample.

steps.title: Aliasing
steps.body:
If f_s < 2f_m, spectral copies overlap: a tone at f appears at |f − kf_s| (the alias within 0…f_s/2).
Example: CD audio samples at 44.1 kHz to cover up to ~20 kHz hearing range with room for a practical anti-alias filter.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** x(t) = cos(200πt) + sin(600πt): f_m = 300 Hz ⇒ Nyquist rate 600 Hz.

**Example 2.** A 7 kHz tone sampled at 10 kHz appears at |7 − 10| = 3 kHz.

**Example 3.** Signal sinc²-type with bandwidth 5 kHz multiplied by a 20 kHz carrier — highest frequency 25 kHz ⇒ Nyquist rate 50 kHz (for low-pass sampling).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using ω (rad/s) and f (Hz) interchangeably.
- Taking f_m as the carrier frequency instead of carrier + bandwidth.
- Thinking anti-aliasing filters go after the sampler (they must come before).

quiz.why: The Nyquist rate is twice the highest frequency: 2 × 4 kHz = 8 kHz.
An anti-aliasing filter band-limits the signal before the sampler, so frequencies above f_s/2 cannot alias.
An ideal reconstruction filter is a low-pass filter with cut-off f_s/2. It removes the spectral images.

quiz.why: Sampling with an impulse train makes the spectrum repeat every f_s. So it is periodic in frequency with period f_s.

courses.title: Analog Electronics · Unit 1 · Diodes and their applications
courses.summary: PN junction, diode equation and models, half-wave, full-wave and bridge rectifiers with ripple and PIV, capacitor filters, Zener regulators, clippers, clampers and voltage multipliers.
outcomes: Use ideal, constant-drop and exponential diode models
Analyse rectifiers: Vdc, ripple factor, efficiency, PIV
Design a capacitor filter and a Zener shunt regulator
Analyse clippers and clampers
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: Inside every adapter, diodes turn AC into DC.
They conduct one way — and the details of that 'one way' matter.

steps.title: Junction physics
steps.body: Diffusion of carriers creates a depletion region and barrier potential (~0.7 V Si, ~0.3 V Ge). Forward bias narrows it — current rises exponentially; reverse bias widens it — tiny saturation current I_s until breakdown (avalanche or Zener).

steps.title: Diode equation and models
steps.body:
I = I_s(e^(V/(ηV_T)) − 1), V_T = kT/q ≈ 25.9 mV at 300 K, η = 1–2.
Models: ideal (short/open), constant drop (0.7 V), piecewise linear (0.7 V + r_f). Dynamic resistance r_d = ηV_T/I_D (≈ 26 mV/I_D). Current doubles for about every 18 mV (η = 1)… roughly ×10 per 60 mV.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 5 V source, 1 kΩ, Si diode (0.7 V): I = 4.3 mA.

**Example 2.** r_d at I_D = 2 mA (η = 1): 26/2 = 13 Ω.

**Example 3.** I_s = 10⁻¹⁴ A, V = 0.65 V, η = 1: I = 10⁻¹⁴·e^(25.1) ≈ 0.8 mA.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming the diode conducts when the anode is below the cathode by less than 0.7 V.
- Using the ideal model when the supply is only a few volts (error is large).
- Forgetting temperature: V_D falls ~2 mV/°C.

activity.prompt: 12 V supply, 1.13 kΩ resistor, Si diode (0.7 V drop). Current in mA?

quiz.why: The barrier (cut-in) potential of silicon is about 0.7 V (germanium about 0.3 V).
The thermal voltage V_T = kT/q ≈ 26 mV at 300 K.
The reverse saturation current is very small, since it comes from minority carriers.
The dynamic resistance is r_d = V_T/I = 26 mV/1 mA = 26 Ω.

quiz.q: Forward drop changes with temperature by
quiz.why: The forward voltage of a silicon diode drops by about 2 mV for each °C rise in temperature.

scenes.text: A hobbyist builds a 12 V DC supply from a transformer, diodes and a capacitor.
The capacitor smooths the bumps; ripple decides the capacitor size.

steps.title: Rectifier formulas (ideal diodes, resistive load, V_m peak)
steps.body:
- **Half-wave:** V_dc = V_m/π, I_rms = I_m/2, ripple factor 1.21, efficiency 40.6%, PIV = V_m, ripple at f.
- **Centre-tap full-wave:** V_dc = 2V_m/π, ripple factor 0.482, efficiency 81.2%, PIV = 2V_m, ripple at 2f.
- **Bridge:** V_dc = 2V_m/π, PIV = V_m, two diode drops per half-cycle, no centre tap needed.

steps.title: Capacitor filter
steps.body: Peak-to-peak ripple V_r ≈ I_dc/(fC) (half-wave) or I_dc/(2fC) (full-wave). V_dc ≈ V_m − V_r/2. Ripple factor ≈ 1/(4√3 fCR) for full-wave.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 230/12 V RMS transformer, bridge, ideal diodes: V_m = 16.97 V ⇒ V_dc = 10.8 V; with 0.7 V drops: V_m′ = 15.57 V.

**Example 2.** Full-wave with I_dc = 0.5 A, f = 50 Hz, ripple 1 V p-p: C = 0.5/(100 × 1) = 5000 µF.

**Example 3.** Half-wave, V_m = 20 V, R = 1 kΩ: V_dc = 6.37 V, I_dc = 6.37 mA, PIV = 20 V.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using RMS instead of peak values in V_dc formulas.
- Forgetting two diode drops in a bridge.
- Choosing diodes with PIV below 2V_m in a centre-tap rectifier.

quiz.why: For a full-wave rectifier, V_dc = 2V_m/π, about 0.637V_m.

quiz.q: Ripple frequency of a 50 Hz bridge rectifier
quiz.why: A bridge rectifier produces two pulses per input cycle, so the ripple frequency is twice 50 Hz = 100 Hz.
A larger capacitor holds the voltage better between pulses, so ripple is reduced. Ripple is proportional to 1/C.
A half-wave rectifier's diode must withstand the peak input in reverse, so PIV = V_m.
The maximum efficiency of a full-wave rectifier is 81.2% (a half-wave one is 40.6%).

scenes.text: A temperature sensor needs a steady 5.1 V even when the battery sags.
A Zener diode in reverse breakdown holds the voltage nearly constant.

steps.title: Zener shunt regulator
steps.body:
Source V_s through series R to the Zener (reverse-biased) in parallel with the load. In breakdown, V_Z ≈ constant. I_R = (V_s − V_Z)/R = I_Z + I_L.
Design: keep I_Z ≥ I_Z,min at minimum V_s and maximum I_L; check P_Z = V_Z I_Z,max ≤ rating at maximum V_s and minimum I_L.
Line regulation = ΔV_o/ΔV_s; load regulation = (V_NL − V_FL)/V_FL × 100%.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** V_s = 12 V, V_Z = 5.1 V, R = 330 Ω, R_L = 1 kΩ: I_R = 20.9 mA, I_L = 5.1 mA, I_Z = 15.8 mA, P_Z = 81 mW.

**Example 2.** If R_L is removed: I_Z = 20.9 mA, P_Z = 107 mW (worst case for the Zener).

**Example 3.** Minimum R_L for regulation with I_Z,min = 1 mA: I_L,max = 19.9 mA ⇒ R_L,min = 5.1/0.0199 = 256 Ω.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forward-biasing the Zener (it then acts as an ordinary 0.7 V diode).
- Ignoring the no-load case when checking power.
- Forgetting that the Zener stops regulating if V_s falls too low.

activity.prompt: Zener regulator: Vs = 15 V, Vz = 6 V, R = 450 Ω, no load. Zener current (mA)?

quiz.why: A Zener diode is used in reverse breakdown, where the voltage stays almost constant. That is how it regulates.

quiz.q: I_R in a shunt regulator equals
quiz.why: By KCL, the current through the series resistor splits into the Zener current and the load current: I_R = I_Z + I_L.
The Zener current is largest when the supply voltage is highest and the load current is lowest. That gives the worst-case power.
options: max V_s and min load current

quiz.q: Zener breakdown dominates for V_Z below about
quiz.why: Below about 5–6 V, Zener (tunnelling) breakdown dominates. Above, avalanche breakdown dominates.

quiz.q: Line regulation measures change in V_o due to
quiz.why: Line regulation measures how much the output changes when the input (line) voltage changes.

scenes.text: A 3.3 V microcontroller input must survive a 12 V spike.
A clipper with diodes to the rails cuts the excess.

steps.title: Clippers
steps.body: Series or shunt diodes (with bias V_B) remove parts of a waveform above/below a level. Positive shunt clipper with bias V_B: output limited to V_B + 0.7 V. Double clipper (two diodes, two biases) limits both sides.

steps.title: Clampers and multipliers
steps.body:
Clamper (C + diode + R, RC ≫ T) shifts the DC level without changing shape: positive clamper puts the negative peak at ≈ 0 (or bias), output swings 0 to 2V_m.
Voltage doubler (half-wave): two diodes + two capacitors ⇒ ≈ 2V_m; tripler/quadrupler by cascading stages.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 10 V peak sine into a shunt clipper with diode + 3 V battery (Si): output clipped at 3.7 V on the positive side.

**Example 2.** Positive clamper on a 5 V peak square wave: output 0 to 10 V (ideal).

**Example 3.** Doubler from a 12 V RMS secondary: ≈ 2 × 16.97 = 33.9 V DC (ideal, light load).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the 0.7 V drop in the clipping level.
- Choosing RC comparable to the period in a clamper (it then distorts).
- Confusing clipper (changes shape) with clamper (shifts level).

items.text: Removes the part of the signal above 5 V
Shifts a waveform so its minimum sits at 0 V
Needs a capacitor with RC ≫ T
Limits both peaks with two diodes

quiz.why: A clamper shifts the DC level of a signal without changing its shape.

quiz.q: Shunt clipper with 2 V bias (Si) clips at
quiz.why: A shunt clipper clips when the diode conducts: bias plus the 0.7 V drop. So 2 V + 0.7 V = 2.7 V.

quiz.q: Ideal positive clamper output for ±V_m input
quiz.why: An ideal positive clamper shifts the whole waveform up so its negative peak is at 0. A ±V_m input becomes 0 to 2V_m.
A voltage doubler charges a capacitor to V_m and adds it to the next peak. The output is about 2V_m.
A clamper needs a long discharge time, RC ≫ T, so the capacitor keeps its charge across the cycle.

questions.why: A diode conducts when forward biased with a voltage above its cut-in value (about 0.7 V for silicon).

questions.q: Number of diodes in a bridge rectifier
questions.why: A bridge rectifier uses 4 diodes.
A Zener diode is mainly used for voltage regulation.
For a half-wave rectifier, V_dc = V_m/π = 31.4/3.14 = 10 V.
A half-wave rectifier gives one pulse per cycle, so the ripple frequency equals the supply frequency, 60 Hz.
r_d = V_T/I = 26 mV/0.5 mA = 52 Ω.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Centre-tap rectifier diodes need PIV of 2V_m.  Reason (R): When one diode conducts, the other sees both half-windings in reverse.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: In a centre-tap rectifier, when one diode conducts, the other sees the whole secondary voltage in reverse, i.e. 2V_m. So the PIV is 2V_m and R explains A.

questions.q: C for full-wave ripple 2 V p-p at 1 A, 50 Hz
questions.why: For a full-wave rectifier, ripple V_r = I/(2fC). So C = I/(2fV_r) = 1/(2 × 50 × 2) = 0.005 F = 5000 µF.

questions.q: Zener: V_s = 20 V, V_Z = 10 V, R = 500 Ω, R_L = 1 kΩ. I_Z
Bridge with 9 V RMS secondary and 0.7 V diodes: peak output
questions.why: The peak of a 9 V RMS secondary is 9√2 ≈ 12.73 V. A bridge has two diodes in the path, so subtract 1.4 V: ≈ 11.3 V.

questions.q: Case: A 5 V Zener (1 W) is fed from 12 V through 100 Ω with no load. Is it safe?
questions.why: The current is (12 − 5)/100 = 70 mA. Zener power = 5 V × 0.07 A = 0.35 W, which is below the 1 W rating, so it is safe.
options: Yes — P_Z ≈ 0.35 W, below the 1 W rating

questions.q: Minimum R_L for Zener: V_s 15, V_Z 9, R 200 Ω, I_Z,min 5 mA
questions.why: I_R = (15 − 9)/200 = 30 mA. At least 5 mA must flow in the Zener, so the load can take at most 25 mA. Minimum R_L = 9/0.025 = 360 Ω.

questions.q: Diode current with I_s = 10⁻¹³ A at 0.6 V (V_T = 25 mV)
Ripple factor of full-wave with capacitor: f = 50, C = 1000 µF, R = 100 Ω
questions.why: For a full-wave rectifier with capacitor, r = 1/(4√3 fCR) = 1/(4 × 1.732 × 50 × 10⁻³ × 100) = 1/34.6 ≈ 0.0289.

questions.q: Diode current rises about 10× for each additional
questions.why: From I = I_s e^(V/V_T), the current rises 10× for each ΔV = V_T ln 10 ≈ 26 mV × 2.3 ≈ 60 mV.

courses.title: Analog Electronics · Unit 2 · Bipolar junction transistors and amplifiers
courses.summary: BJT structure and operation, configurations and characteristics, operating regions, DC load line and biasing (fixed, collector-feedback, voltage-divider) with stability, small-signal hybrid-π and re models, and CE, CC, CB amplifier analysis.
outcomes: Identify active, saturation and cut-off regions
Bias a BJT stably with the voltage-divider method
Draw the small-signal model and compute gain, R_in, R_out
Compare CE, CC and CB amplifiers
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: A microcontroller pin (a few mA) switches a 200 mA LED strip through a transistor.
A small base current controls a much larger collector current.

steps.title: Operation
steps.body:
NPN: emitter (heavily doped) injects electrons into a thin base; most reach the collector. I_E = I_B + I_C; I_C = βI_B = αI_E; α = β/(β + 1).
Regions: **active** (BE forward, BC reverse) — amplifier; **saturation** (both forward, V_CE ≈ 0.2 V) — switch ON; **cut-off** (both reverse) — switch OFF.
Early effect: I_C rises slightly with V_CE (output resistance r_o = V_A/I_C).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** β = 100, I_B = 20 µA: I_C = 2 mA, I_E = 2.02 mA, α = 0.990.

**Example 2.** Switch: V_CC = 12 V, LED load R_C = 60 Ω ⇒ I_C(sat) ≈ (12 − 0.2 − 2)/60 ≈ 0.16 A (2 V LED). With β = 100 need I_B > 1.6 mA; drive 3 mA for hard saturation (R_B = (5 − 0.7)/3 mA ≈ 1.4 kΩ from a 5 V pin).

steps.title: Configurations
steps.body: CE (common emitter): voltage and current gain, phase inversion. CB: voltage gain, current gain ≈ 1, low input resistance. CC (emitter follower): voltage gain ≈ 1, high input, low output resistance — buffer.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming I_C = βI_B in saturation (it is less).
- Swapping α and β.
- Forgetting the base–emitter drop (≈ 0.7 V) when finding I_B.

activity.prompt: β = 150 and I_C = 3 mA. Base current in µA?

quiz.why: By KCL, the emitter current is the sum of the base and collector currents: I_E = I_B + I_C.
In the active region, the base–emitter junction is forward biased and the base–collector junction is reverse biased.
An emitter follower (common collector) has voltage gain close to 1. It is used as a buffer.
A transistor used as a switch is ON in saturation, where V_CE is about 0.2 V.

scenes.text: An amplifier designed in winter distorts on hot afternoons.
β and V_BE change with temperature; good biasing keeps the Q-point steady.

steps.title: Load line and Q-point
steps.body:
DC load line: V_CE = V_CC − I_C(R_C + R_E). Q-point (I_CQ, V_CEQ) near the middle for maximum symmetric swing.
Fixed bias: I_B = (V_CC − 0.7)/R_B — Q-point depends strongly on β (poor).
Voltage-divider bias: Thevenin V_TH = V_CC R₂/(R₁ + R₂), R_TH = R₁ ∥ R₂; I_B = (V_TH − 0.7)/(R_TH + (β + 1)R_E). If βR_E ≥ 10R₂, I_C ≈ (V_TH − 0.7)/R_E — nearly independent of β.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** V_CC = 12 V, R₁ = 47 kΩ, R₂ = 10 kΩ, R_C = 2.2 kΩ, R_E = 1 kΩ, β = 100.
V_TH = 2.105 V, R_TH = 8.25 kΩ; I_B = 1.405/(8.25k + 101k) = 12.9 µA; I_C = 1.29 mA (approx. method: 1.405 mA).
V_CE = 12 − 1.29(3.2) = 7.9 V ⇒ active ✔.

**Example 2.** Fixed bias with R_B = 470 kΩ, V_CC = 12, β = 100 vs 200: I_C = 2.4 mA vs 4.8 mA — Q-point doubles (unstable).

steps.title: Stability factor
steps.body: S = ∂I_C/∂I_CO. Fixed bias S = β + 1 (poor); voltage divider S ≈ 1 + R_TH/R_E (good when small). Thermal runaway: rising I_C heats the junction ⇒ more I_C; R_E feedback prevents it.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ignoring (β + 1)R_E reflected into the base.
- Placing the Q-point near saturation.
- Forgetting to check V_CE > V_CE(sat).

items: Find V_TH and R_TH of the divider
Write base loop: V_TH = I_B R_TH + 0.7 + (β + 1)I_B R_E
Solve for I_B, then I_C = βI_B
Compute V_CE = V_CC − I_C R_C − I_E R_E
Confirm the transistor is in the active region

quiz.why: The voltage-divider bias with an emitter resistor gives negative feedback, so the Q-point is the most stable.

quiz.q: DC load line end on V_CE axis
quiz.why: On the DC load line, I_C = 0 at V_CE = V_CC. That is the point on the V_CE axis.
For fixed bias, the stability factor is about β + 1, which is poor (large) because the collector current varies a lot with β and temperature.

quiz.q: R_E reflected into the base loop as
quiz.why: The emitter current is (β + 1) times the base current. So R_E appears in the base loop as (β + 1)R_E.
The emitter resistor gives negative feedback. If current rises, voltage across R_E rises and reduces base drive, preventing thermal runaway.

lessons.title: Small-signal models and the CE amplifier

scenes.text: A microphone gives a few millivolts; a CE stage amplifies it 100 times.
The small-signal model predicts that gain.

steps.title: Hybrid-π / re model
steps.body:
g_m = I_C/V_T (≈ I_C/26 mV); r_π = β/g_m; r_e = V_T/I_E ≈ 26 mV/I_E; r_o = V_A/I_C.
h-parameters (CE): h_ie ≈ r_π, h_fe ≈ β.

steps.title: CE amplifier (R_E bypassed)
steps.body:
A_v = −g_m(R_C ∥ R_L ∥ r_o) ≈ −(R_C ∥ R_L)/r_e. R_in = R₁ ∥ R₂ ∥ r_π. R_out ≈ R_C.
Unbypassed R_E (degeneration): A_v ≈ −R_C/(r_e + R_E) — lower but more stable gain, higher R_in = R₁ ∥ R₂ ∥ (β + 1)(r_e + R_E).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** I_C = 1.3 mA: g_m = 50 mA/V; r_e = 20 Ω; β = 100 ⇒ r_π = 2 kΩ. R_C = 2.2 kΩ, R_L = 10 kΩ (R_E bypassed): A_v = −50m × (2.2k ∥ 10k = 1.8k) = −90.
R_in = 47k ∥ 10k ∥ 2k = 1.6 kΩ.

**Example 2.** With R_E = 1 kΩ unbypassed: A_v ≈ −1.8k/1.02k ≈ −1.8.

**Example 3.** Emitter follower, R_E = 1 kΩ: A_v = R_E/(r_e + R_E) ≈ 0.98.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using DC resistances in AC analysis without shorting capacitors and DC sources.
- Forgetting the load R_L in parallel with R_C.
- Dropping the minus sign (phase inversion) of the CE stage.

activity.prompt: I_C = 2.6 mA. Transconductance g_m = I_C/26 mV in mA/V?

quiz.why: The transconductance g_m = I_C/V_T, where V_T ≈ 26 mV.
The input resistance r_π = β/g_m, since g_m = I_C/V_T and I_B = I_C/β.
A common-emitter stage inverts the signal, giving a 180° phase shift.
A bypass capacitor across R_E makes the emitter AC ground. That removes AC feedback and raises the AC gain, while the DC bias stays the same.
An emitter follower has high input and low output resistance with gain near 1. So it works as a buffer.

lessons.title: CB, CC stages, multistage and frequency response basics

scenes.text: A hi-fi amplifier has a pre-amp, driver and buffer stages.
Cascading stages multiplies gains — and each stage's R_in loads the previous one.

steps.title: Comparison
steps.body:
| | CE | CB | CC |
Voltage gain: high, high, ≈ 1
Current gain: β, α ≈ 1, β + 1
R_in: medium, low (≈ r_e), high
R_out: high (≈ R_C), high, low
Phase: 180°, 0°, 0°

Cascade: A_total = A₁A₂…, with each stage loaded by the next stage's R_in. In dB, gains add: 20 log|A|.

steps.title: Frequency response
steps.body: Low-frequency roll-off from coupling and bypass capacitors (f_L ≈ 1/(2πR_eqC)); high-frequency roll-off from junction capacitances and the Miller effect (C_M = C_μ(1 + |A_v|) at the input of a CE stage). Bandwidth = f_H − f_L; gain–bandwidth trade-off.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Two stages with gains −40 and −25: total 1000 (60 dB), in phase.

**Example 2.** Coupling cap: R_in = 1.6 kΩ, want f_L = 20 Hz ⇒ C = 1/(2π·20·1600) ≈ 5 µF.

**Example 3.** Miller: C_μ = 2 pF, A_v = −90 ⇒ C_M = 182 pF — dominates the input capacitance.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Multiplying unloaded gains of stages.
- Forgetting the Miller multiplication in CE stages.
- Adding gains in linear form instead of dB.

quiz.why: Gain in dB = 20 log₁₀(100) = 40 dB.
The common-collector (emitter follower) stage has the highest input resistance, about (β + 1) times the emitter load. CE is medium, and CB is very low.
At low frequencies, the coupling and bypass capacitors act as high impedances and limit the gain. They set the low-frequency cut-off. Junction capacitances limit the high end.

quiz.q: Total gain of stages 20 dB and 30 dB
quiz.why: Gains in decibels add for cascaded stages. 20 dB + 30 dB = 50 dB.

quiz.q: Miller capacitance for C = 5 pF, A_v = −49
quiz.why: Miller effect: the effective input capacitance is C(1 + |A_v|) = 5 × (1 + 49) = 250 pF.

questions.why: The emitter is heavily doped so it can inject many carriers into the base. The base is thin and lightly doped.
Current gain β is the ratio of collector current to base current, I_C/I_B.
A common-collector (CC) amplifier is also called an emitter follower, because the emitter voltage follows the base.
The emitter resistance r_e = V_T/I_E = 26 mV/1 mA = 26 Ω.

questions.q: V_CE(sat) of a small Si BJT
questions.why: In saturation a small silicon BJT has V_CE(sat) of about 0.2 V.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Voltage-divider bias with a large R_E makes I_C nearly independent of β.  Reason (R): With βR_E ≫ R_TH, I_C ≈ (V_TH − V_BE)/R_E.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

scenes.text: A phone processor holds billions of MOSFETs.
Their gate draws almost no current — ideal for dense, low-power logic.

steps.title: JFET
steps.body: Voltage-controlled: I_D = I_DSS(1 − V_GS/V_P)² for V_P ≤ V_GS ≤ 0 (n-channel). Gate–channel junction reverse biased ⇒ very high input resistance. g_m = (2I_DSS/|V_P|)(1 − V_GS/V_P).

steps.title: MOSFET (n-channel enhancement)
steps.body:
Insulated gate (SiO₂ or high-k). Channel forms for V_GS > V_T (threshold).
- Cut-off: V_GS < V_T, I_D ≈ 0.
- Triode (linear): V_DS < V_GS − V_T, I_D = k′(W/L)[(V_GS − V_T)V_DS − V_DS²/2].
- Saturation: V_DS ≥ V_GS − V_T, I_D = ½k′(W/L)(V_GS − V_T)² (1 + λV_DS).
Depletion MOSFET has a built-in channel (conducts at V_GS = 0).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** JFET I_DSS = 10 mA, V_P = −4 V, V_GS = −2 V: I_D = 10(0.5)² = 2.5 mA; g_m = (20/4)(0.5) = 2.5 mS.

**Example 2.** MOSFET k′W/L = 2 mA/V², V_T = 1 V, V_GS = 3 V, V_DS = 5 V: saturation (5 > 2) ⇒ I_D = ½·2·4 = 4 mA.

**Example 3.** Same with V_DS = 1 V: triode ⇒ I_D = 2[(2)(1) − 0.5] = 3 mA.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the saturation equation without checking V_DS ≥ V_GS − V_T.
- Sign errors for p-channel devices.
- Confusing BJT 'saturation' (switch on) with MOSFET 'saturation' (constant-current, amplifier region).

activity.prompt: JFET: I_DSS = 12 mA, V_P = −6 V, V_GS = −3 V. I_D (mA)?

quiz.why: A FET's drain current is controlled by the gate voltage, so it is a voltage-controlled device. A BJT is current-controlled.
A MOSFET is in saturation (pinch-off) when V_DS ≥ V_GS − V_T. Below that, it is in the triode region.
At V_GS = 0 a JFET carries its maximum drain current, I_DSS (Shockley equation).
An enhancement MOSFET has no channel at V_GS = 0. It conducts only when V_GS exceeds the threshold V_T.
The MOSFET gate is insulated by an oxide layer, so the gate current is practically zero.

story.title: Bias for a radio front end

scenes.text: An FM receiver's front end uses a JFET for low noise.
Self-bias sets V_GS automatically through a source resistor.

steps.title: Methods
steps.body:
**JFET self-bias:** V_GS = −I_D R_S; solve with Shockley (quadratic, pick root with V_P < V_GS < 0).
**Voltage-divider (MOSFET/JFET):** V_G = V_DD R₂/(R₁ + R₂); V_GS = V_G − I_D R_S; solve with the device equation.
Drain feedback for enhancement MOSFETs: V_GS = V_DS (always saturated).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1 (self-bias).** I_DSS = 8 mA, V_P = −4 V, R_S = 1 kΩ: I_D = 8(1 − I_D/4)² (I_D in mA) ⇒ I_D² − 10I_D + 16 = 0 ⇒ I_D = 2 mA (8 rejected) ⇒ V_GS = −2 V.

**Example 2 (E-MOSFET divider).** V_DD = 12, V_G = 4 V, R_S = 1 kΩ, ½k′W/L = 1 mA/V², V_T = 1 V: I_D = (4 − I_D − 1)² ⇒ I_D² − 7I_D + 9 = 0 ⇒ I_D = 1.70 mA (other root 5.3 gives V_GS < V_T, reject). V_GS = 2.30 V.

steps.title: Root selection
steps.body: Always reject the root that puts V_GS outside the valid range (beyond pinch-off for JFETs, below V_T for E-MOSFETs).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Keeping both roots.
- Forgetting V_GS = −I_D R_S is negative for n-JFET self-bias.
- Not checking saturation after finding I_D.

items: Write V_GS = −I_D R_S
Substitute into I_D = I_DSS(1 − V_GS/V_P)²
Solve the quadratic for I_D
Reject the root giving |V_GS| > |V_P|
Compute V_DS and check saturation

quiz.why: In JFET self-bias, the drain current through R_S makes the source positive. With the gate at 0 V, V_GS = −I_D R_S.
V_GS = −I_D R_S = −2 mA × 1 kΩ = −2 V.
With the gate tied to the drain, V_DS = V_GS, which is above V_GS − V_T. So the enhancement MOSFET stays in saturation.
Self-bias gives two roots. The valid one has |V_GS| ≤ |V_P| (the JFET is on). A root with |V_GS| > |V_P| would mean the JFET is cut off, so it is rejected.
The FET gate draws negligible current, so a gate divider has only a tiny effect and gives a stable bias with high input resistance.

scenes.text: A pH electrode has megaohms of source resistance.
A FET input stage barely loads it — perfect.

steps.title: Model and stages
steps.body:
Small-signal: g_m (MOSFET sat: g_m = k′(W/L)(V_GS − V_T) = 2I_D/(V_GS − V_T) = √(2k′(W/L)I_D)), r_o = 1/(λI_D).
**Common source (R_S bypassed):** A_v = −g_m(R_D ∥ R_L ∥ r_o); R_in = R_G (divider); R_out ≈ R_D.
**CS with unbypassed R_S:** A_v = −g_mR_D/(1 + g_mR_S).
**Source follower (CD):** A_v = g_mR_S/(1 + g_mR_S) < 1; R_out ≈ 1/g_m ∥ R_S.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** g_m = 2 mS, R_D = 5 kΩ, R_L = 20 kΩ: A_v = −2m × 4k = −8.

**Example 2.** Unbypassed R_S = 1 kΩ: A_v = −2m × 5k/(1 + 2) = −3.33.

**Example 3.** Source follower R_S = 2 kΩ, g_m = 4 mS: A_v = 8/9 = 0.89; R_out ≈ 250 Ω ∥ 2k = 222 Ω.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using BJT formulas with r_π for FETs (FET input is open).
- Forgetting R_L in parallel with R_D.
- Calculating g_m from the triode equation for a saturated device.

activity.prompt: CS amplifier: g_m = 3 mS, R_D ∥ R_L = 4 kΩ (R_S bypassed). |A_v|?

quiz.why: A common-source amplifier has voltage gain A_v = −g_m R_D, an inverting stage.
A source follower has gain slightly below 1, so it works as a buffer.

quiz.q: FET amplifier input resistance is set mainly by
quiz.why: The gate takes no current, so the amplifier's input resistance is set mainly by the gate bias resistors.

quiz.q: g_m for I_D = 2 mA, V_GS − V_T = 1 V
quiz.why: For a MOSFET in saturation, g_m = 2I_D/V_ov = 2 × 2 mA/1 V = 4 mS.
An unbypassed R_S gives source degeneration (negative feedback). It lowers the gain but makes it more stable.

lessons.title: MOSFET as a switch and the CMOS inverter

scenes.text: A laptop CPU flips billions of CMOS switches every second.
CMOS draws power mainly while switching — that is why it dominates digital design.

steps.title: CMOS inverter
steps.body:
PMOS from V_DD to output, NMOS from output to ground, gates tied together. Input high ⇒ NMOS on, PMOS off ⇒ output 0. Input low ⇒ PMOS on ⇒ output V_DD. Static current ≈ 0 (only leakage).
Voltage-transfer characteristic: switching threshold ≈ V_DD/2 for matched devices; noise margins NM_H = V_OH − V_IH, NM_L = V_IL − V_OL.

steps.title: Power and switching
steps.body: Dynamic power P = αC_L V_DD² f (α = activity factor). Halving V_DD cuts dynamic power to one quarter — why chips use low supply voltages. Power MOSFET switch: conduction loss I²R_DS(on); use a gate driver for fast switching; flyback diode across inductive loads.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** C_L = 10 fF, V_DD = 1 V, f = 2 GHz, α = 0.1: P = 0.1 × 10⁻¹⁴ × 1 × 2×10⁹ = 2 µW per gate.

**Example 2.** MOSFET with R_DS(on) = 20 mΩ carrying 10 A: P = 2 W ⇒ needs a heat sink.

**Example 3.** Same circuit at V_DD = 0.8 V instead of 1 V: dynamic power × 0.64.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Driving a relay coil from a MOSFET without a flyback diode.
- Thinking CMOS has zero power (dynamic and leakage power exist).
- Leaving MOSFET gates floating (they pick up charge and switch unpredictably).

statements.s: A CMOS inverter draws large static current.
Dynamic power is proportional to V_DD².
A flyback diode protects a switch driving an inductor.
NMOS conducts when its gate is low.

quiz.q: When CMOS inverter input is high
quiz.why: When a CMOS inverter's input is high, the NMOS turns on and the PMOS turns off. The output is pulled low.
CMOS dynamic power is P = αC V_DD² f, with activity factor α, load capacitance C and frequency f.

quiz.q: Conduction loss of a MOSFET switch
quiz.why: When a MOSFET switch is on, it behaves like a small resistance R_DS(on). The conduction loss is I² R_DS(on).

quiz.q: Halving V_DD changes dynamic power by
quiz.why: Dynamic power depends on V_DD². Halving the supply voltage gives (1/2)² = 1/4 of the power.
The high noise margin is NM_H = V_OH − V_IH: how much the output high level can drop and still be read as high.

questions.why: The FET gate is insulated or reverse-biased, so the input resistance is very high.
CMOS (complementary MOS) uses NMOS and PMOS transistors together.
The JFET pinch-off voltage is written V_P.

MOSFET (½k′W/L = 0.5 mA/V², V_T = 2 V) at V_GS = 4 V, saturated: I_D

questions.why: V_ov = V_GS − V_T = 2 V. Saturation needs V_DS ≥ 2 V, but V_DS = 1 V, so it is in the triode region.

questions.q: Assertion (A): MOSFET 'saturation' is the region used for amplification.  Reason (R): In saturation, I_D is nearly independent of V_DS.

questions.why: I = 9(1 − I/3)² ⇒ I² − 7I + 9 = 0 ⇒ I ≈ 1.70 mA (the 5.30 mA root gives |V_GS| > |V_P|).

questions.why: A logic-level N-MOSFET can be turned fully on by 3.3 V, with a low R_DS(on). A flyback diode protects against the solenoid's inductive spike.

courses.title: Analog Electronics · Unit 4 · Op-amps, feedback and oscillators
courses.summary: Ideal and practical op-amp parameters, inverting, non-inverting, summing, difference and instrumentation amplifiers, integrator and differentiator, comparators and Schmitt trigger, negative feedback topologies and their effects, and oscillators using the Barkhausen criterion (RC phase-shift, Wien bridge, LC).
outcomes: Analyse op-amp circuits using virtual short
Design inverting/non-inverting/summing/difference amplifiers
Explain effects of negative feedback on gain, bandwidth and impedances
Design RC phase-shift and Wien-bridge oscillators
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: A weighing scale's strain gauge gives millivolts.
An op-amp with two resistors sets an exact, stable gain.

steps.title: Ideal op-amp and golden rules
steps.body: Infinite open-loop gain, infinite R_in, zero R_out, infinite bandwidth. With negative feedback: (1) V₊ = V₋ (virtual short), (2) input currents = 0.

steps.title: Basic configurations
steps.body:
- **Inverting:** A_v = −R_f/R₁; R_in = R₁.
- **Non-inverting:** A_v = 1 + R_f/R₁; R_in very high.
- **Voltage follower:** A_v = 1.
- **Summing (inverting):** V_o = −R_f(V₁/R₁ + V₂/R₂ + …).
- **Difference:** with R₁ = R₃, R_f = R₄: V_o = (R_f/R₁)(V₂ − V₁).
- **Instrumentation amp (3 op-amp):** gain = (1 + 2R/R_G)(R₃/R₂), high CMRR, high R_in.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Inverting R₁ = 10 kΩ, R_f = 100 kΩ, V_in = 0.2 V: V_o = −2 V.

**Example 2.** Non-inverting R₁ = 1 kΩ, R_f = 9 kΩ: gain 10.

**Example 3.** Summing R_f = 10 kΩ, R₁ = R₂ = 10 kΩ, V₁ = 1 V, V₂ = 2 V: V_o = −3 V (an audio mixer).

**Example 4.** Output saturates near the rails: with ±12 V supplies and gain 100, a 0.2 V input would clip at about ±11 V.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying the virtual short to circuits without negative feedback (comparators).
- Forgetting the 1 in the non-inverting gain.
- Ignoring output saturation at the supply rails.

activity.prompt: Non-inverting amplifier: R₁ = 2 kΩ, R_f = 18 kΩ, V_in = 0.3 V. V_o (V)?

quiz.why: An inverting op-amp amplifier has gain −R_f/R₁.
With negative feedback and a high open-loop gain, the two inputs sit at nearly the same voltage, V₊ ≈ V₋. This is the virtual short.
A voltage follower has gain 1. It copies the input and works as a buffer.

quiz.q: Summing amp with R_f = R = 10 k, inputs 0.5 V and 1.5 V
quiz.why: The summing amplifier output is −(R_f/R)(V₁ + V₂) = −(0.5 + 1.5) = −2 V.
Instrumentation amplifiers have high common-mode rejection and very high input impedance, so they suit small sensor signals.

lessons.title: Integrator, differentiator, comparators and practical parameters

scenes.text: A function generator makes triangles by integrating square waves.
A comparator with hysteresis makes the squares.

steps.title: Integrator and differentiator
steps.body: Integrator: V_o = −(1/RC)∫V_in dt (add R_f across C to limit DC gain). Differentiator: V_o = −RC dV_in/dt (add series R to limit high-frequency gain/noise).

steps.title: Comparators and Schmitt trigger
steps.body: Open-loop comparator: output ±V_sat depending on sign of V₊ − V₋. Schmitt trigger (positive feedback) has two thresholds: V_UT, V_LT = ±βV_sat with β = R₂/(R₁ + R₂) (inverting type, symmetric supplies); hysteresis V_H = 2βV_sat — rejects noise.

steps.title: Practical parameters
steps.body: Input offset voltage, bias current, CMRR = A_d/A_cm (dB), **slew rate** SR (V/µs): full-power bandwidth f_max = SR/(2πV_p). Gain–bandwidth product GBW constant for a dominant-pole op-amp (e.g. 1 MHz): closed-loop bandwidth = GBW/noise gain.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Integrator R = 10 kΩ, C = 0.1 µF, V_in = +1 V step: ramp of −1000 V/s (−1 V per ms) until saturation.

**Example 2.** Schmitt: R₁ = 9 kΩ, R₂ = 1 kΩ, V_sat = ±12 V: thresholds ±1.2 V, hysteresis 2.4 V.

**Example 3.** SR = 0.5 V/µs, 10 V peak output: f_max = 0.5×10⁶/(2π·10) ≈ 8 kHz.

**Example 4.** GBW 1 MHz, gain 100: bandwidth 10 kHz.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Expecting full output swing at high frequency despite slew-rate limits.
- Using negative-feedback rules for a Schmitt trigger.
- Forgetting the minus sign of the inverting integrator.

quiz.why: An integrator integrates its input. A constant input gives a linear ramp at the output.

quiz.q: Hysteresis width of Schmitt (β = 0.1, V_sat = ±10 V)
quiz.why: The Schmitt trigger's hysteresis width is 2βV_sat = 2 × 0.1 × 10 = 2 V.
The full-power bandwidth is the highest frequency at which a full-amplitude sine is not slew-limited: f_max = SR/(2πV_p).

quiz.q: Closed-loop BW for GBW 2 MHz, gain 20
quiz.why: Closed-loop bandwidth = GBW/gain = 2 MHz/20 = 100 kHz.
Comparators work in open loop or with positive feedback, driving the output into saturation. They do not use the linear region.

scenes.text: Raw transistor gain varies with temperature and part tolerance.
Feeding back a fraction of the output trades some gain for accuracy and bandwidth.

steps.title: Basic feedback equation
steps.body: A_f = A/(1 + Aβ). Loop gain T = Aβ. If Aβ ≫ 1, A_f ≈ 1/β (set by passive components). Desensitivity D = 1 + Aβ: dA_f/A_f = (1/D)·dA/A. Bandwidth × D; distortion and noise inside the loop ÷ D.

steps.title: Topologies (sampling–mixing)
steps.body:
- Voltage-series (series–shunt): voltage amplifier — R_in ×D, R_out ÷D (non-inverting op-amp).
- Current-series: transconductance — R_in ×D, R_out ×D.
- Voltage-shunt: transresistance — R_in ÷D, R_out ÷D (inverting op-amp).
- Current-shunt: current amplifier — R_in ÷D, R_out ×D.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** A = 10⁵, β = 0.01: A_f = 10⁵/1001 ≈ 99.9.

**Example 2.** If A drops 50% to 5×10⁴: A_f = 5×10⁴/501 = 99.8 — only 0.1% change.

**Example 3.** Amplifier BW 10 kHz, D = 100 ⇒ closed-loop BW ≈ 1 MHz.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking feedback increases gain (negative feedback reduces it).
- Mixing up which topology raises or lowers R_in/R_out.
- Ignoring stability: too much phase shift turns negative feedback into positive (oscillation).

quiz.why: With feedback, the closed-loop gain is A_f = A/(1 + Aβ).
When Aβ ≫ 1, the closed-loop gain approaches 1/β, which depends only on the passive feedback network.
A non-inverting op-amp samples the output voltage and mixes the feedback in series with the input. That is the voltage-series topology.
Negative feedback keeps the gain–bandwidth product constant, so bandwidth increases by (1 + Aβ) as gain falls by the same factor.

quiz.q: Excess loop phase shift can cause
quiz.why: If the loop phase shift grows too large at a frequency where loop gain is still at least 1, negative feedback becomes positive. The circuit can oscillate.

scenes.text: Every radio and microcontroller needs a stable oscillator.
An amplifier with positive feedback of exactly the right gain and phase sustains a sine wave.

steps.title: Barkhausen criterion
steps.body: |Aβ| = 1 and ∠Aβ = 0° (or 360°) at the oscillation frequency. In practice |Aβ| slightly > 1 to start, with amplitude limiting (non-linearity, AGC, lamp/thermistor).

steps.title: Common circuits
steps.body:
- **RC phase-shift (3 equal RC sections, inverting amp):** f = 1/(2πRC√6); β = 1/29 ⇒ amplifier gain ≥ 29.
- **Wien bridge (non-inverting amp):** f = 1/(2πRC); β = 1/3 ⇒ gain ≥ 3 (R_f = 2R₁).
- **LC (Colpitts):** f = 1/(2π√(L C_eq)), C_eq = C₁C₂/(C₁ + C₂). **Hartley:** L_eq = L₁ + L₂ (+2M).
- **Crystal:** very high Q, frequency stability ~ppm — used for clocks.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Wien bridge R = 10 kΩ, C = 16 nF: f = 1/(2π × 1.6×10⁻⁴) ≈ 995 Hz; set R_f = 2R₁ (slightly more for start-up).

**Example 2.** RC phase-shift R = 10 kΩ, C = 10 nF: f = 1/(2π × 10⁻⁴ × 2.449) ≈ 650 Hz; need |A| ≥ 29.

**Example 3.** Colpitts L = 100 µH, C₁ = C₂ = 2 nF: C_eq = 1 nF ⇒ f ≈ 503 kHz.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using gain exactly = 3 (Wien) — oscillation won't start reliably; use slightly more with limiting.
- Forgetting √6 in the phase-shift formula.
- Adding Colpitts capacitances directly (they are in series).

activity.prompt: Wien-bridge oscillator: R = 1 kΩ, C = 0.159 µF. Frequency (Hz, ≈)?

quiz.why: The Barkhausen criterion for sustained oscillation is |Aβ| = 1 and a loop phase shift of 0° (or 360°).
The Wien bridge feedback network attenuates by 1/3 at the oscillation frequency. So the amplifier needs a gain of at least 3.
An RC phase-shift network attenuates by 1/29 at the oscillation frequency, so the amplifier gain must be at least 29.
A crystal has a very high Q, giving excellent frequency stability. The tuning range is small.

quiz.q: Colpitts C_eq for 1 nF and 1 nF
quiz.why: The two capacitors are in series: C_eq = (1 × 1)/(1 + 1) = 0.5 nF.

questions.why: An ideal op-amp has infinite input resistance, so it draws no input current.

questions.q: Inverting amp R₁ = 1 k, R_f = 47 k: gain
questions.why: The inverting gain is −R_f/R₁ = −47 k/1 k = −47.
Oscillators use positive feedback so the output sustains itself, with loop gain 1 and zero phase shift.

questions.q: Difference amp (R_f/R₁ = 5), V₂ = 1.2 V, V₁ = 1.0 V: V_o
questions.why: The difference amplifier output is (R_f/R₁)(V₂ − V₁) = 5 × (1.2 − 1.0) = 1 V.
CMRR in dB = 20 log₁₀(100,000) = 20 × 5 = 100 dB.

questions.q: Integrator R = 100 kΩ, C = 1 µF, V_in = −0.5 V for 2 s: ΔV_o
Assertion (A): Negative feedback reduces gain sensitivity to component changes.  Reason (R): A_f ≈ 1/β depends only on passive components when loop gain is large.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: With high loop gain, A_f ≈ 1/β, set by passive components. So the gain hardly changes when the active device varies, i.e. lower sensitivity. R explains A.

steps.title: Positional systems
steps.body: Value = Σ dᵢ × baseⁱ. Decimal → binary: repeated division by 2 (integer part), repeated multiplication by 2 (fraction). Binary ↔ octal: group 3 bits; binary ↔ hex: group 4 bits from the binary point.

steps.title: Binary arithmetic
steps.body: Addition rules 0+0 = 0, 1+1 = 10 (carry). Subtraction via complements. Multiplication = shift and add.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reading remainders top-down instead of bottom-up.
- Grouping bits from the wrong end.
- Using digits ≥ base (e.g. 8 in octal).

activity.prompt: Write a function to_bin(n) that converts a non-negative integer to a binary string WITHOUT using bin(); print to_bin(45).
activity.starter:
def to_bin(n):
    if n == 0:
        return '0'
    s = ''
    # repeated division by 2
    return s

print(to_bin(45))
activity.hint: Prepend n % 2 to the string and integer-divide n by 2 until it becomes 0.

quiz.why: 25 = 16 + 8 + 1, so in binary it is 11001.
Group the bits in 3s: 111 101 is 7 and 5, so the octal number is 75.
Group in 4s: 1011 = B and 1110 = E, so the hex is BE.

steps.title: Representations (n bits)
steps.body:
- Sign-magnitude: MSB sign; range −(2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1)…+(2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1); two zeros.
- 1's complement: invert all bits; two zeros.
- **2's complement:** invert and add 1; range −2ⁿ⁻¹…+(2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1); one zero. 8-bit: −128 to +127.
Subtraction A − B = A + (2's complement of B); discard the final carry.
Overflow: adding two numbers of the same sign gives a result of the opposite sign (carry into MSB ≠ carry out).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to add 1 for 2's complement.
- Treating the final carry as part of the answer.
- Missing overflow when signs agree.

activity.text: Range is ___ to +127, and −1 is written as ___ (8 bits).

quiz.why: To get the 2's complement of 0101, invert it to 1010 and add 1, giving 1011.
−1 in 8-bit 2's complement is all ones: 11111111.
1's complement has two zeros, +0 (all 0s) and −0 (all 1s). That is its weakness.
Overflow can occur when adding two numbers of the same sign, if the result goes out of range and has the wrong sign. Numbers of opposite sign cannot overflow.
options: two numbers of the same sign

quiz.why: The leading 1 means negative. Invert 11110110 to get 00001001 and add 1 to get 00001010 = 10. So the value is −10.

lessons.title: Codes: BCD, Gray, excess-3, parity and ASCII

scenes.text: A volume knob's position sensor uses Gray code.
Only one bit changes between positions, so no glitchy readings.

steps.title: Codes
steps.body:
- **BCD (8421):** each decimal digit in 4 bits (1010–1111 invalid). 59 = 0101 1001.
- **Excess-3:** BCD + 0011 (self-complementing).
- **Gray code:** g = b ⊕ (b >> 1); successive values differ in one bit. Gray→binary: b_MSB = g_MSB, bᵢ = bᵢ₊₁ ⊕ gᵢ.
- **Parity:** even parity makes the total number of 1s even — detects single-bit errors.
- **ASCII:** 7-bit character code ('A' = 65 = 1000001, '0' = 48).
- Hamming code adds parity bits to correct single-bit errors.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Binary 1011 → Gray 1110 (1, 1⊕0, 0⊕1, 1⊕1).

**Example 2.** Gray 1101 → binary 1001 (1; 1⊕1 = 0; 0⊕0 = 0; 0⊕1 = 1).

**Example 3.** BCD addition 7 + 5: 0111 + 0101 = 1100 (> 9) ⇒ add 0110 ⇒ 1 0010 = 12 in BCD.

**Example 4.** Even-parity bit for 1011001: four 1s ⇒ parity 0.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Converting a whole number to binary instead of digit-by-digit for BCD.
- Forgetting the +6 correction in BCD addition.
- Gray→binary: XOR with the previous *binary* bit, not the previous Gray bit.

activity.prompt: Print the 4-bit Gray code of the number 11 (binary 1011) using g = b ^ (b >> 1), formatted as 4 bits.
activity.hint: Use the XOR operator ^ and right shift >>.

quiz.why: BCD encodes each decimal digit in 4 bits. 4 is 0100 and 7 is 0111, so 47 is 0100 0111.
Gray code: the first bit is the same, and each next bit is the XOR of adjacent binary bits. 0110 gives 0, 0⊕1 = 1, 1⊕1 = 0, 1⊕0 = 1, i.e. 0101.
Excess-3 is BCD plus 3. 5 + 3 = 8 = 1000.
The ASCII code of 'A' is 65 (hex 41).
A single parity bit detects any single-bit error, but cannot correct it and may miss 2-bit errors.

scenes.text: A chip designer cuts a 10-gate circuit to 4 gates — less area, power and delay.
Boolean algebra and K-maps find the simplest form.

steps.title: Laws
steps.body:
Identity A + 0 = A, A·1 = A; null A + 1 = 1, A·0 = 0; idempotent A + A = A; complement A + A′ = 1, AA′ = 0; absorption A + AB = A, A(A + B) = A; A + A′B = A + B; consensus AB + A′C + BC = AB + A′C.
**De Morgan:** (A + B)′ = A′B′, (AB)′ = A′ + B′. NAND and NOR are universal gates.

steps.title: Canonical forms and K-maps
steps.body: SOP minterms Σm(…), POS maxterms ΠM(…). K-map: Gray-ordered cells; group 1, 2, 4, 8 adjacent 1s (wrapping at edges), as large as possible; each group gives a product term; don't-cares (X) may be used to enlarge groups.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** F = AB + AB′ + A′B = A + A′B = A + B.

**Example 2.** F(A,B,C) = Σm(0, 2, 4, 5, 6): group m0, m2, m4, m6 (the C′ column pair, corners) ⇒ C′; group m4, m5 ⇒ AB′. F = C′ + AB′.

**Example 3.** F(A,B,C,D) = Σm(1, 3, 5, 7, 9) + d(11, 13, 15): quad m1, m3, m5, m7 ⇒ A′D; with don't-cares, the octet of all odd minterms ⇒ F = D.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing K-map columns in binary order (00, 01, 10, 11) instead of Gray (00, 01, 11, 10).
- Missing wrap-around groups at the edges and corners.
- Forcing don't-cares to be 1 when they don't help.

quiz.why: NAND and NOR are universal gates. Any logic function can be built from either one alone.
A variable ANDed with its complement is always 0: A·A′ = 0.
K-map cells are arranged in Gray code order so that neighbouring cells differ by one bit. That allows grouping.

quiz.q: Group of 4 ones in a 4-variable K-map eliminates
quiz.why: A group of 4 = 2² cells eliminates 2 variables, since 2 of the variables change within the group.
The sum of all four minterms of a 2-variable function is 1.

questions.why: Hexadecimal is base 16.
De Morgan's law: (AB)′ = A′ + B′.
8 = 2³, which is 1000 in binary.
Gray of 1000: keep the first bit 1, then 1⊕0 = 1, 0⊕0 = 0, 0⊕0 = 0, giving 1100.

questions.q: Assertion (A): 2's complement allows subtraction with an adder.  Reason (R): A − B = A + (B′ + 1).
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: In 2's complement, A − B = A + (B′ + 1), so a single adder can do subtraction. That is what simplifies hardware.
Combine terms: A′B′C + A′BC = A′C, and A′B′C + AB′C = B′C. The expression simplifies to A′C + B′C.
8 + 7 = 15, which is above 9, so add 6 for BCD correction. 15 becomes 0001 0101 (decimal 15).
2C₁₆ = 44 and 1F₁₆ = 31. 44 + 31 = 75, which is 4B in hex.
Minterms 1, 3, 5, 7 are all those where C = 1. So F = C.

questions.q: Case: 8-bit signed adder computes 01111111 + 00000001. Result and flag
questions.why: 127 + 1 = 128, which does not fit in 8-bit signed. The result 10000000 means −128, with overflow set.
Minterms 0, 2, 8, 10 are the four corners of the K-map. They share B = 0 and D = 0, so F = B′D′.

questions.q: Minimum NAND gates to implement XOR
questions.why: An XOR gate can be built from 4 two-input NAND gates, which is the classic minimum.
The minterms 0–7 cover the half of the map where A = 0, and the don't-care at 8 does not help. So F = A′.

scenes.text: Every CPU adds numbers billions of times per second.
It starts with a full adder: three input bits, sum and carry out.

steps.title: Half and full adder
steps.body:
Half adder: S = A ⊕ B, C = AB.
Full adder: S = A ⊕ B ⊕ Cᵢₙ, C_out = AB + Cᵢₙ(A ⊕ B) (= AB + BCᵢₙ + ACᵢₙ). Built from two half adders and an OR gate.
Half subtractor: D = A ⊕ B, Borrow = A′B. Full subtractor: D = A ⊕ B ⊕ Bᵢₙ, B_out = A′B + Bᵢₙ(A ⊕ B)′.

steps.title: Multi-bit adders
steps.body: Ripple-carry: n full adders chained — delay grows linearly with n. **Carry look-ahead:** generate Gᵢ = AᵢBᵢ, propagate Pᵢ = Aᵢ ⊕ Bᵢ; Cᵢ₊₁ = Gᵢ + PᵢCᵢ, expanded so all carries are computed in parallel (two-level logic). Adder–subtractor: XOR each B bit with a mode line M and set C₀ = M.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** A = 1, B = 1, Cᵢₙ = 1: S = 1, C_out = 1.

**Example 2.** 4-bit ripple adder, each full adder carry delay 2 gate delays ⇒ ~8 gate delays for the carry chain.

**Example 3.** C₂ in look-ahead: C₂ = G₁ + P₁G₀ + P₁P₀C₀.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing C_out = A ⊕ B.
- Forgetting C₀ = 1 when subtracting with the 2's-complement method.
- Confusing propagate (XOR) with generate (AND).

activity.prompt: Write full_adder(a, b, cin) returning (sum, carry) using ^, & and |. Print full_adder(1, 1, 1) and full_adder(1, 0, 0).
activity.starter:
def full_adder(a, b, cin):
    s = 0
    c = 0
    return s, c

print(full_adder(1, 1, 1))
print(full_adder(1, 0, 0))
activity.solution:
def full_adder(a, b, cin):
    s = a ^ b ^ cin
    c = (a & b) | (cin & (a ^ b))
    return s, c

print(full_adder(1, 1, 1))
print(full_adder(1, 0, 0))
activity.hint: Sum is the XOR of all three; carry is ab OR cin(a XOR b).

quiz.why: A half adder's sum is A XOR B, and its carry is AB.
A full adder can be built from two half adders and an OR gate for the carry.
options: two half adders and an OR gate

quiz.why: A carry look-ahead adder computes all carries in parallel from the generate and propagate terms. It does not wait for a ripple.
A half subtractor's borrow is A′B: a borrow is needed when A = 0 and B = 1.
The propagate signal is P_i = A_i ⊕ B_i. It shows that a carry in is passed on.

scenes.text: Several sensors share one ADC channel through a selector.
A multiplexer picks one of many inputs using select lines.

steps.title: MUX and DEMUX
steps.body:
2ⁿ:1 MUX has n select lines: Y = Σ mᵢ Iᵢ (minterm of selects × data). 4:1 MUX: Y = S₁′S₀′I₀ + S₁′S₀I₁ + S₁S₀′I₂ + S₁S₀I₃.
DEMUX 1:2ⁿ routes one input to the selected output (a decoder with enable).
Trees: 8:1 from two 4:1 + one 2:1.

steps.title: Function implementation with a MUX
steps.body: An n-variable function can be built with a 2ⁿ⁻¹:1 MUX: use n − 1 variables as selects; each data input is 0, 1, the last variable or its complement (from the implementation table).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** F(A,B,C) = Σm(1, 2, 6, 7) with a 4:1 MUX, selects A, B: AB = 00 → m0, m1 ⇒ I₀ = C; 01 → m2, m3 ⇒ I₁ = C′; 10 → m4, m5 ⇒ I₂ = 0; 11 → m6, m7 ⇒ I₃ = 1.

**Example 2.** 16:1 MUX needs 4 select lines; from 4:1 MUXes: five devices (four + one).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Wrong order of select lines (MSB vs LSB).
- Forgetting the enable input on cascaded devices.
- Counting data inputs wrongly (2ⁿ for n selects).

activity.prompt: Number of select lines for a 32:1 multiplexer?

quiz.why: An 8:1 MUX has 8 inputs, so it needs log₂ 8 = 3 select lines.
A demultiplexer sends one input to one of several outputs. It is equivalent to a decoder with an enable input used as data.
A 16:1 MUX built from 4:1 MUXes needs 4 in the first layer and 1 in the second: 5.

quiz.q: MUX implementing a 4-variable function needs at least
quiz.why: A 4-variable function can be implemented with an 8:1 MUX (n − 1 select lines), using the 4th variable on the data inputs.
For the MUX table, both minterms of the pair (6 and 7) are 1 for I₃, so I₃ = 1 regardless of the last variable.

scenes.text: A digital clock turns BCD digits into lit segments.
A decoder maps each code to exactly one active output.

steps.title: Decoders and encoders
steps.body:
n:2ⁿ decoder: each output is one minterm — with an OR gate it implements any SOP function. Enable inputs allow cascading (two 3:8 → one 4:16).
Encoder 2ⁿ:n: output is the code of the active input. **Priority encoder** gives the highest-priority active input and a valid bit.
BCD-to-7-segment decoder drives displays (common anode or cathode).

steps.title: Magnitude comparator
steps.body: 1-bit: (A > B) = AB′, (A < B) = A′B, (A = B) = (A ⊕ B)′. Multi-bit: equality xᵢ = (Aᵢ ⊕ Bᵢ)′; A = B ⇔ all xᵢ; A > B = A₃B₃′ + x₃A₂B₂′ + x₃x₂A₁B₁′ + …

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Full adder with a 3:8 decoder: S = Σm(1, 2, 4, 7), C = Σm(3, 5, 6, 7) — two OR gates on decoder outputs.

**Example 2.** 4:2 priority encoder with inputs D₃ (highest)…D₀: D₂ = 1, D₁ = 1 ⇒ output 10 (D₂ wins), valid = 1.

**Example 3.** Compare A = 1011, B = 1001: x₃ = 1, x₂ = 1, A₁B₁′ = 1 ⇒ A > B.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ignoring active-low outputs (common in IC decoders).
- Ordinary encoders give wrong codes for multiple active inputs (need priority).
- Forgetting the valid/enable line.

items.text: Gives code of the active input
Outputs A > B, A = B, A < B

quiz.why: A 4:16 decoder has 2⁴ = 16 outputs.
A priority encoder handles several active inputs at once, by outputting the code of the highest-priority one.
A 1-bit equality output is high when A = B. That is XNOR, (A ⊕ B)′.
A 4:16 decoder can be made from two 3:8 decoders, using the extra input bit as an enable for each.
A decoder gives all minterms. An OR gate over the minterms of a function implements any sum-of-products function.

scenes.text: A display flickers a wrong digit for a few nanoseconds when inputs change.
That is a hazard — caused by unequal path delays — and can be removed with redundant terms.

steps.title: Code converters
steps.body:
Design steps: truth table (inputs → outputs, unused codes as don't-cares), K-map each output, implement.
- BCD → excess-3: add 0011.
- Binary → Gray: gᵢ = bᵢ₊₁ ⊕ bᵢ (XOR chain).
- Gray → binary: bᵢ = bᵢ₊₁ ⊕ gᵢ (cascaded XORs).

steps.title: Hazards
steps.body:
Static-1 hazard: output should stay 1 but glitches to 0 during an input change (SOP with adjacent groups not overlapping). Fix: add the consensus term covering the transition.
Static-0 hazard: dual for POS. Dynamic hazard: multiple transitions when one is expected (multi-level circuits).
Example: F = AB + A′C has a static-1 hazard when B = C = 1 and A changes; add BC.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 4-bit binary → Gray: g₃ = b₃, g₂ = b₃ ⊕ b₂, g₁ = b₂ ⊕ b₁, g₀ = b₁ ⊕ b₀ (3 XOR gates).

**Example 2.** BCD to excess-3 output E₃ = B₃ + B₂B₀ + B₂B₁ (using don't-cares 10–15).

**Example 3.** Hazard-free F = AB + A′C + BC.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Leaving unused BCD combinations as 0 instead of don't-cares (bigger circuits).
- Assuming minimal SOP is always hazard-free.
- Cascading XORs in the wrong direction for Gray → binary.

items: State the problem and assign input/output variables
Write the truth table (mark don't-cares)
