quiz.why: For a 4-bit binary-to-Gray conversion, the MSB passes through and the other 3 bits each need one XOR, so 3 XOR gates.
A static-1 hazard is removed by adding the consensus (redundant) term, which covers the transition between two product terms.

quiz.q: Unused BCD codes are treated as
quiz.why: Unused BCD codes (10–15) never occur, so they are treated as don't-cares to simplify the logic.
Hazards come from unequal propagation delays through different paths. They cause brief glitches.
For F = AB + A′C, adding the consensus term BC gives a hazard-free form: AB + A′C + BC.

questions.why: A full adder has 3 inputs: A, B and the carry in.

questions.q: MUX with 2 select lines has data inputs
questions.why: A multiplexer with 2 select lines can choose among 2² = 4 data inputs.
Each decoder output is high for exactly one input combination, so each is a minterm.

questions.q: Carry out of a full adder for 1, 0, 1
questions.why: Carry out = AB + Cin(A ⊕ B). For A = 1, B = 0, Cin = 1: 0 + 1·1 = 1.

questions.q: Gray code is obtained from binary using
questions.why: Gray code is obtained by XORing adjacent bits of the binary number.

questions.q: 2:4 decoder with enable can act as
questions.why: A 2:4 decoder with an enable input can act as a 1:4 demultiplexer, with the data on the enable and the select on the address inputs.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Carry look-ahead adders reduce delay compared with ripple-carry.  Reason (R): They compute every carry from G and P terms in two levels of logic.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: A look-ahead adder computes every carry in parallel from G and P in two logic levels, so no ripple delay builds up. So R explains A.

questions.q: Implement F(A,B,C) = Σm(0, 3, 5, 6) with 3:8 decoder: OR of outputs
questions.why: A decoder gives one output per minterm. To implement F = Σm(0, 3, 5, 6), OR the outputs 0, 3, 5 and 6.
A = 0110 and B = 0111 differ only in the last bit, where A has 0 and B has 1. So A < B.

questions.q: 8:1 MUX implementing F(A,B,C,D) uses selects A, B, C. If minterms 6 and 7 are 1 (ABC = 011), I₃ =
questions.why: With the selects ABC = 011, minterms 6 and 7 are both 1 for D = 0 and D = 1. So I₃ = 1.

questions.q: Case: A 4-bit adder must work at 1 GHz but ripple delay is 1.6 ns. Best fix
questions.why: Ripple carry delay is too long at 1 GHz. A carry look-ahead adder computes carries in parallel, shortening the critical path.

questions.q: Ripple adder of 16 bits with 2-gate-delay carry per bit: worst-case carry delay
questions.why: The carry ripples through 16 bits at 2 gate delays each: 16 × 2 = 32 gate delays.

questions.q: Number of 2:1 MUXes to build a 16:1 MUX
questions.why: A 16:1 MUX tree of 2:1 MUXes needs 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 15.

questions.q: Priority encoder (D₇ highest) with D₅ and D₂ high outputs
questions.why: The priority encoder outputs the code of the highest active input. D₅ is higher than D₂, so the output is 5 = 101.

questions.q: Static hazard in F = AB′ + BC occurs when A = C = 1 and B changes; fix by adding
questions.why: For F = AB′ + BC with A = C = 1, B changes and a static-1 hazard occurs. Adding the consensus term AC covers the transition.

courses.title: Digital Electronics · Unit 3 · Sequential circuits
courses.summary: Latches and flip-flops (SR, D, JK, T, master–slave and edge-triggered), characteristic and excitation tables, timing parameters, shift registers, asynchronous and synchronous counters, and design of synchronous sequential circuits (Moore/Mealy state machines).
outcomes: Explain latch and flip-flop operation and timing
Use characteristic and excitation tables
Design registers and synchronous/asynchronous counters
Design simple Moore and Mealy state machines
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: Every register in a CPU is a row of flip-flops.
They store one bit and change only on a clock edge.

steps.title: Latches
steps.body: SR latch (cross-coupled NOR): S = 1 sets Q = 1, R = 1 resets, S = R = 0 holds, S = R = 1 invalid (NOR). Gated D latch: Q follows D while enable is high (transparent) — a problem in synchronous systems.

steps.title: Flip-flops and characteristic equations
steps.body:
Edge-triggered (sample at the clock edge):
- D: Q⁺ = D
- JK: Q⁺ = JQ′ + K′Q (J = K = 1 toggles)
- T: Q⁺ = T ⊕ Q
- SR: Q⁺ = S + R′Q (SR = 0)
Master–slave JK removes the race-around problem of level-triggered JK.
Timing: setup time t_su, hold time t_h, clock-to-Q t_cq. Max clock f_max = 1/(t_cq + t_logic + t_su).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** JK with J = 1, K = 1, Q = 0 ⇒ after edge Q = 1 (toggle).

**Example 2.** T flip-flop with T = 1 halves the clock frequency (divide-by-2).

**Example 3.** t_cq = 1 ns, logic 6 ns, t_su = 1 ns ⇒ f_max = 125 MHz.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating a latch as edge-triggered.
- Violating setup/hold times (metastability).
- Forgetting that S = R = 1 is forbidden for SR.

quiz.why: A JK flip-flop with J = K = 1 toggles on every clock edge.
A D latch is level-sensitive. It is transparent (follows D) when its enable is high.
Race-around happens in a level-triggered JK with J = K = 1. It is avoided by master–slave or edge-triggered flip-flops.
The minimum clock period is t_cq + logic + t_su = 2 + 8 + 2 = 12 ns. So f_max = 1/12 ns ≈ 83 MHz.

quiz.q: T flip-flop with T = 1 acts as
quiz.why: A T flip-flop with T = 1 toggles each clock edge, so its output frequency is half of the clock: divide by 2.

scenes.text: A lab only has JK flip-flops but the design needs a D flip-flop.
Excitation tables let you convert one type into another.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** JK → D: J = D, K = D′.

**Example 2.** JK → T: J = K = T.

**Example 3.** D → T: D = T ⊕ Q.

**Example 4.** SR → JK: S = JQ′, R = KQ.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: Write the required next state from the target flip-flop's characteristic table, look up the excitation of the available flip-flop, K-map each input in terms of the target inputs and Q.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the characteristic table where the excitation table is required.
- Ignoring don't-cares in JK excitation (they simplify a lot).
- Forgetting Q as a K-map variable.

activity.text: JK to T: J = K = ___ ; D to T: D = T ⊕ ___.

quiz.why: For a JK flip-flop 0 → 1, J must be 1 and K can be anything (X): J = 1, K = X.
For 1 → 1 (no change), T must be 0.
A JK flip-flop acts as a D flip-flop with J = D and K = D′.
The excitation table gives the inputs needed to make a given state transition. The characteristic table gives the next state for given inputs.
For an SR flip-flop 1 → 0, S = 0 and R = 1 (reset).

scenes.text: A watch divides a 32 768 Hz crystal down to 1 Hz.
A chain of 15 toggle stages (÷2¹⁵) does exactly that.

steps.title: Registers
steps.body: Shift registers: SISO, SIPO, PISO, PIPO; universal shift register (shift left/right, parallel load). Ring counter (n flip-flops, n states, one-hot). Johnson (twisted-ring) counter: 2n states.

steps.title: Counters
steps.body:
**Asynchronous (ripple):** each flip-flop clocked by the previous output; simple but delays accumulate (glitches in decoding). Mod-N: reset at count N using a NAND on the outputs.
**Synchronous:** all flip-flops share the clock; T inputs: T₀ = 1, T₁ = Q₀, T₂ = Q₀Q₁, … (up counter). Design arbitrary sequences with excitation tables and K-maps.
Number of flip-flops for mod-N: smallest n with 2ⁿ ≥ N.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 32 768 Hz ÷ 2¹⁵ = 1 Hz ⇒ 15 flip-flops.

**Example 2.** Mod-10 ripple counter: 4 flip-flops, reset when Q₃Q₁ = 1 (count 1010).

**Example 3.** 3-bit synchronous up counter with T flip-flops: T₀ = 1, T₁ = Q₀, T₂ = Q₁Q₀.

**Example 4.** 4-bit Johnson counter: 8 states 0000 → 1000 → 1100 → 1110 → 1111 → 0111 → 0011 → 0001.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Decoding ripple-counter outputs without accounting for glitches.
- Choosing too few flip-flops for mod-N.
- Mixing ring (n states) and Johnson (2n states).

activity.prompt: Flip-flops needed for a mod-50 counter?

quiz.why: A 4-bit ring counter circulates a single 1, so it has 4 states.
An n-bit Johnson counter has 2n states. For 4 bits, 8 states.
A synchronous counter clocks all flip-flops together. So the delays do not add up as they do in a ripple counter.
A mod-6 counter has 6 states, which need 3 flip-flops since 2³ = 8 ≥ 6.
SIPO means Serial-In, Parallel-Out. It converts a serial stream to parallel outputs.

scenes.text: A digital lock opens only when the bits 1-0-1 arrive in order.
A finite-state machine remembers how much of the pattern it has seen.

steps.title: Moore vs Mealy
steps.body:
Moore: outputs depend only on present state (output changes on clock edge; may need more states). Mealy: outputs depend on state and input (fewer states, output can change between edges).
Design steps: state diagram → state table → state minimisation → state assignment → excitation table → K-maps → circuit.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1 (Mealy 101 detector, overlapping).** States: S0 (nothing), S1 (got 1), S2 (got 10).
S0: x = 1 → S1/0; x = 0 → S0/0. S1: x = 0 → S2/0; x = 1 → S1/0. S2: x = 1 → S1/1 (detected, overlap keeps the final 1); x = 0 → S0/0. Two flip-flops suffice.

**Example 2.** A Moore version needs a fourth state S3 (detected) whose output is 1.

**Example 3.** Input 1 0 1 0 1: Mealy outputs 0 0 1 0 1 (detections at the 3rd and 5th bits).

steps.title: State assignment and minimisation
steps.body: n flip-flops encode up to 2ⁿ states; equivalent states (same outputs, same next-state classes) can be merged; good assignments place related states at adjacent codes to simplify logic; one-hot encoding (one flip-flop per state) is popular in FPGAs.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting overlap handling in sequence detectors.
- Moore outputs drawn on transitions (they belong to states).
- Leaving unused states without a safe next state (lock-up).

activity.prompt: Simulate the overlapping Mealy '101' detector: for input '10101' print the output string.
activity.starter:
def detect(bits):
    state = 0  # 0: none, 1: got 1, 2: got 10
    out = ''
    for b in bits:
        # update state and append '1' or '0'
        pass
    return out

print(detect('10101'))
activity.hint: Track three states; output 1 only when in 'got 10' and the input is 1.

quiz.why: In a Moore machine, the outputs depend only on the present state.
Mealy outputs depend on the state and input, so a Mealy machine usually needs fewer states than the equivalent Moore machine.
5 states need ⌈log₂ 5⌉ = 3 flip-flops with binary encoding (2³ = 8 ≥ 5).
One-hot encoding uses one flip-flop per state, with exactly one set at a time.
Unused states should lead back to a valid state, so the machine cannot get stuck (lock-up) after a glitch.

questions.why: A flip-flop stores 1 bit.
A D flip-flop's next state equals the input D: Q⁺ = D.
In an asynchronous (ripple) counter, each flip-flop is clocked by the output of the previous one.

questions.q: Clock 1 MHz into a 4-bit ripple counter: MSB frequency
questions.why: A 4-bit counter divides by 2⁴ = 16 at the MSB. So 1 MHz/16 = 62.5 kHz.

questions.q: Invalid input of NOR SR latch
questions.why: For a NOR SR latch, S = R = 1 is invalid, since it forces both outputs to 0, and releasing both gives an unpredictable result.
A T flip-flop toggles when T = 1. Using a D flip-flop, D = T ⊕ Q.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Ripple counters can produce decoding glitches.  Reason (R): Flip-flops change one after another, so outputs pass through intermediate states.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: In a ripple counter, flip-flops change one after another. The outputs pass through brief intermediate states, which cause glitches when decoded. So R explains A.
A mod-12 counter needs 4 flip-flops, since 2⁴ = 16 ≥ 12.
In a synchronous up counter, the 4th bit toggles only when all lower bits are 1. So T₃ = Q₀Q₁Q₂.

questions.q: f_max: t_cq 0.5 ns, logic 3 ns, t_su 0.5 ns
questions.why: T_min = t_cq + logic + t_su = 0.5 + 3 + 0.5 = 4 ns. So f_max = 250 MHz.

questions.q: Case: A 10 MHz clock must produce a 1 kHz tick. Ideal divide ratio and minimum flip-flops (binary counter mod-N)
questions.why: 10 MHz/1 kHz = 10,000. A binary counter needs ⌈log₂ 10,000⌉ = 14 flip-flops (2¹⁴ = 16,384 ≥ 10,000).
For a JK flip-flop staying at 1 (1 → 1), J can be anything and K must be 0: J = X, K = 0.

questions.q: Johnson counter 3-bit state after 001 (shift right, Q₀ = complement of Q₂ fed back) starting 000 → 100 → 110 → 111 → 011 → ?
questions.why: The Johnson sequence is 000, 100, 110, 111, 011, 001, then back to 000. So after 011 comes 001.
For input 1101101, the pattern 101 is completed at positions 4 and 7. So the output is 0001001.

questions.q: Minimum states for a Moore '11' detector (overlapping)
questions.why: A Moore detector for 11 (overlapping) needs states for: no progress, seen one 1, and seen 11 (output 1). That is 3 states.

courses.title: Digital Electronics · Unit 4 · Logic families, memories and data converters
courses.summary: Logic family parameters (fan-out, noise margin, propagation delay, power, figure of merit), TTL and CMOS basics, open-collector/tri-state outputs, semiconductor memories (ROM, PROM, EPROM, flash, SRAM, DRAM) and memory expansion, PLDs, and DAC/ADC types and specifications.
outcomes: Compare logic families using standard parameters
Explain tri-state and open-drain outputs
Classify memories and design memory expansion
Compute DAC/ADC resolution and conversion times
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

lessons.title: Logic family parameters, TTL and CMOS

scenes.text: A 5 V sensor board must talk to a 3.3 V microcontroller.
Logic levels and noise margins decide whether they understand each other.

steps.title: Parameters
steps.body:
- V_OH(min), V_OL(max), V_IH(min), V_IL(max); noise margins NM_H = V_OH − V_IH, NM_L = V_IL − V_OL
- Fan-out = min(I_OH/I_IH, I_OL/I_IL)
- Propagation delay t_pd = (t_PHL + t_PLH)/2
- Power dissipation; speed–power product (figure of merit) = t_pd × P

steps.title: Families
steps.body:
**TTL (74 series):** BJT-based, 5 V, V_OH 2.4, V_OL 0.4, V_IH 2.0, V_IL 0.8 ⇒ NM 0.4 V; totem-pole output.
**CMOS (74HC, 4000):** very low static power, wide supply range, high fan-out (capacitive limit), NM ≈ 30–45% of V_DD.
**ECL:** fastest classic family, non-saturating, high power.
Open-collector/open-drain outputs allow wired-AND and level shifting (need pull-up). Tri-state outputs (0, 1, high-Z) allow bus sharing.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** TTL: NM_H = 2.4 − 2.0 = 0.4 V; NM_L = 0.8 − 0.4 = 0.4 V.

**Example 2.** Fan-out with I_OL = 16 mA, I_IL = 1.6 mA; I_OH = 400 µA, I_IH = 40 µA ⇒ 10.

**Example 3.** t_pd = 10 ns, P = 10 mW ⇒ speed–power product 100 pJ.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Driving a 3.3 V input with 5 V without checking tolerance.
- Leaving CMOS inputs floating.
- Connecting totem-pole outputs together (bus contention).

activity.prompt: I_OL = 8 mA, I_IL = 0.4 mA, I_OH = 0.4 mA, I_IH = 20 µA. Fan-out?

quiz.why: The high noise margin is NM_H = V_OH − V_IH.
CMOS has the lowest static power, as one transistor is always off, so almost no current flows when not switching.
A tri-state output has a third state, high impedance (Hi-Z), where it is effectively disconnected. This lets many drivers share a bus.
Open-collector outputs cannot pull the line high themselves, so they need an external pull-up resistor.
The speed–power product is delay times power, which has units of energy (joules, e.g. pJ).

scenes.text: Your phone keeps photos in flash memory and runs apps from DRAM.
Each memory type trades speed, density, cost and volatility.

steps.title: Types
steps.body:
- **ROM** (mask), **PROM** (one-time), **EPROM** (UV erase), **EEPROM** (electrical, byte-wise), **Flash** (block erase; NAND for storage, NOR for code) — non-volatile.
- **SRAM:** 6-transistor cell (latch), fast, no refresh, used for caches.
- **DRAM:** 1 transistor + 1 capacitor, dense, needs periodic refresh (charge leaks), main memory.
Volatile = loses data without power (SRAM, DRAM).

steps.title: Organisation and expansion
steps.body: A memory with k address lines and n data lines stores 2ᵏ × n bits. **Word-size expansion:** chips in parallel share address lines (e.g. two 1K×4 → 1K×8). **Capacity expansion:** extra address lines feed a decoder that selects chips (e.g. four 1K×8 → 4K×8 with a 2:4 decoder).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 64K × 8 memory: 16 address lines, 8 data lines, 512 Kbit.

**Example 2.** Build 8K × 16 from 2K × 8 chips: (8/2) × (16/8) = 8 chips; 11 address lines to each chip, 2 more to a 2:4 decoder.

**Example 3.** A 4 Gbit DRAM refreshed every 64 ms across 8192 rows ⇒ one row refresh every ~7.8 µs.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing bits and bytes in capacity.
- Thinking flash is volatile.
- Forgetting the decoder when expanding capacity.

quiz.why: 1M words = 2²⁰, so 20 address lines are needed.
A DRAM cell stores charge on a capacitor, which leaks away. It must be refreshed periodically.
An SRAM cell is a latch made of about 6 transistors. A DRAM cell uses 1 transistor and 1 capacitor.
16K/2K = 8 chips of 2K × 8 are needed.
Flash memory is erased in blocks, but written in smaller units (pages).

scenes.text: A startup prototypes its motor controller logic on an FPGA before making a chip.
Programmable devices let hardware be 'rewritten' like software.

steps.title: PLD families
steps.body:
- **PROM:** fixed AND (decoder), programmable OR — implements any truth table.
- **PLA:** programmable AND and OR arrays — shares product terms.
- **PAL:** programmable AND, fixed OR — faster, simpler.
- **CPLD:** several PAL-like blocks with interconnect, non-volatile.
- **FPGA:** array of look-up tables (LUTs), flip-flops, routing, block RAM, DSP slices — usually SRAM-configured (reloaded at power-up). Designs are written in HDLs (Verilog/VHDL).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** A 4-input LUT stores 16 bits — it can implement any 4-variable function.

**Example 2.** Full adder in a PLA: S needs 4 product terms, C needs 3 (AB, AC_in, BC_in) — 7 terms; with sharing none overlap, so 7 AND terms + 2 OR outputs.

**Example 3.** 3-input, 2-output function in a PROM: 8 × 2 bits.

steps.title: Choosing
steps.body: Small glue logic → CPLD; large/fast parallel designs → FPGA; high-volume products → ASIC (after FPGA prototyping).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing PLA (both arrays programmable) with PAL (only AND programmable).
- Forgetting FPGAs usually need configuration memory at power-up.
- Thinking LUT size limits the total function size (LUTs are combined).

quiz.why: A PAL has a programmable AND array and a fixed OR array. A PROM is the reverse.
A k-input LUT stores the truth table, so it can implement any function of k variables.
SRAM-based FPGAs lose their configuration at power-off, so they load it from external non-volatile memory at power-up.
HDL stands for hardware description language, e.g. Verilog or VHDL.
In a PROM, the AND array is a fixed decoder producing all minterms, and the OR array is programmable.

scenes.text: Your phone's ADC records your voice; its DAC plays music back.
Resolution and speed decide the quality.

steps.title: DAC
steps.body:
Output V_o = V_ref × (D/2ⁿ) (or D × step). Resolution (step) = V_ref/2ⁿ (or full-scale/(2ⁿ − 1)). Types: binary-weighted resistor (needs wide resistor range), **R-2R ladder** (only two resistor values — preferred).
Specs: resolution, accuracy, settling time, linearity, monotonicity.

steps.title: ADC
steps.body:
Quantisation step q = V_FS/2ⁿ; quantisation error ±q/2; ideal SNR ≈ 6.02n + 1.76 dB.
Types: **flash** (2ⁿ − 1 comparators, fastest), **successive approximation (SAR)** (n clock cycles, common in microcontrollers), **dual-slope** (slow, accurate, rejects noise — multimeters), **counter/ramp** (up to 2ⁿ cycles), **sigma-delta** (high resolution audio).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 8-bit DAC, V_ref = 5.12 V: step = 20 mV; D = 100 ⇒ 2.0 V.

**Example 2.** 10-bit SAR ADC at 1 MHz clock: conversion ≈ 10 µs (plus overhead).

**Example 3.** Flash ADC 6-bit needs 63 comparators.

**Example 4.** 12-bit ADC, 3.3 V full scale: q = 0.806 mV; SNR ≈ 74 dB.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using 2ⁿ − 1 vs 2ⁿ inconsistently (state the convention).
- Thinking more bits always mean faster conversion.
- Ignoring the need for an anti-aliasing filter before the ADC.

activity.prompt: 8-bit DAC with V_ref = 2.56 V (step = Vref/256). Output for D = 200 (V)?

quiz.why: A flash ADC compares the input with all thresholds in parallel using many comparators. It is the fastest type.

quiz.q: Comparators in an n-bit flash ADC
quiz.why: An n-bit flash ADC has 2ⁿ levels, needing 2ⁿ − 1 threshold comparators.
A successive-approximation (SAR) ADC does a binary search, deciding one bit per clock. So it takes n clock cycles for n bits.
An R-2R ladder DAC needs only two resistor values, R and 2R, which is easier to match than binary-weighted resistors.

questions.why: DRAM is volatile: it loses its data when power is removed. ROM, EPROM and Flash keep data.
ECL is the fastest of the classic families, because its transistors do not saturate.
A DAC converts a digital code to an analog voltage or current.

questions.q: Step of a 10-bit DAC with V_ref = 10.24 V
questions.why: A 10-bit DAC has 1024 steps. Step size = V_ref/1024 = 10.24/1024 = 10 mV.
A memory with 256K = 2¹⁸ locations needs 18 address lines, because n lines select 2ⁿ locations. The 16 is the data width (bits per word), which does not affect the address count.
The low-level noise margin is NM_L = V_IL − V_OL = 0.8 − 0.4 = 0.4 V. It is how much noise a LOW output can tolerate before the next gate misreads it as HIGH.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Dual-slope ADCs are used in digital multimeters.  Reason (R): They are accurate and average out noise, though slow.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both statements are true. A dual-slope ADC integrates the input over a fixed time, so noise averages out and accuracy is high, but conversion is slow. That is exactly why it suits slowly changing readings in digital multimeters, so R explains A.
Chips needed = (total bits)/(bits per chip) = (16K×8)/(4K×4) = (16/4) rows × (8/4) columns = 4 × 2 = 8. Two chips side by side widen the word to 8 bits, and four such pairs extend the depth to 16K.

questions.q: 12-bit SAR at 2 MHz clock: approx. conversion time
questions.why: A SAR ADC needs one clock cycle per bit, so 12 bits take 12 cycles. With a 2 MHz clock (0.5 µs per cycle), time = 12/2 MHz = 6 µs.
A flash ADC compares the input with every threshold in parallel. An n-bit converter has 2ⁿ levels and so needs 2ⁿ − 1 comparators: 2⁸ − 1 = 255.

questions.q: Case: A 5 V open-drain sensor output must feed a 3.3 V MCU. Correct approach
questions.why: An open-drain output only pulls the line low and relies on a pull-up resistor for the high level. Pulling up to 3.3 V keeps the high level within the MCU's safe range, so the open-drain line does the level shifting. Connecting a 5 V totem-pole output directly could overstress the 3.3 V input.
options: pull-up to 3.3 V on the open-drain line

questions.q: Quantisation error of an 8-bit ADC with 5.12 V full scale
questions.why: Step size q = 5.12 V/2⁸ = 5.12/256 = 20 mV. Quantisation error is at most half a step, ±q/2 = ±10 mV.

questions.q: Speed–power product: t_pd 4 ns, P 2 mW
questions.why: The speed–power product is propagation delay × power: 4 ns × 2 mW = 4×10⁻⁹ × 2×10⁻³ = 8×10⁻¹² J = 8 pJ. Mixing up the prefixes is what gives wrong answers like nJ.

questions.q: DRAM with 8192 rows refreshed every 64 ms: interval between row refreshes
questions.why: All 8192 rows must be refreshed within 64 ms, so one row is refreshed every 64 ms/8192 ≈ 7.8 µs. Dividing in ms and forgetting to convert is the usual slip.

questions.q: Bits of ADC needed for ≈ 74 dB ideal SNR
questions.why: Ideal SNR = 6.02N + 1.76 dB, so N = (74 − 1.76)/6.02 ≈ 12 bits. Each extra bit adds about 6 dB of SNR.

quiz.why: De Morgan's law: the complement of an OR is the AND of the complements, so (A + B)′ = A′B′.
+5 is 0101. Invert to get 1010, then add 1 to get 1011, which is −5 in 4-bit two's complement. Check: 1011 = −8 + 3 = −5.
A half adder adds two bits. The carry is 1 only when both inputs are 1, so Carry = AB (AND). The sum is A ⊕ B.
A 3:8 decoder turns 3 input bits into one of 2³ = 8 output lines, and exactly one is active for each input code.
A D flip-flop copies its D input to the output at the clock edge, so the next state Q⁺ = D, whatever the present Q.
A DRAM cell stores a bit as charge on a capacitor, switched by a single transistor, so it is 1 transistor + 1 capacitor. A 6-transistor cell is SRAM, and a floating gate is used in flash/EPROM.
An n-bit DAC has 2ⁿ input codes. For 8 bits that is 2⁸ = 256 codes (levels). The number of intervals between them would be 255.

questions.why: Octal is base 8, so each digit can be only 0 to 7. The digits 8 and 9 do not exist in octal.
NAND is a universal gate: NOT, AND and OR can all be built from NAND gates alone (for example, tying the inputs together gives NOT). So any logic function can be made with NANDs only.
A ring counter circulates a single 1 through its flip-flops, so n flip-flops give only n states. Five flip-flops give 5 states, not 2⁵ = 32.
A flash ADC uses one comparator per level, all working in parallel, so it converts in one step. That makes it the fastest, but it needs many comparators.
Group the bits in fours from the right: 110110 = 0011 0110 = 3 and 6, so 36 in hex.
Convert Gray to binary: the first bit is copied (0). Each next binary bit = previous binary bit ⊕ next Gray bit: 0⊕1 = 1, 1⊕1 = 0, 0⊕1 = 1. This gives 0101.
A′B + AB′ + AB = A′B + A(B′ + B) = A′B + A = A + B, using the identity A + A′B = A + B. The only input giving 0 is A = B = 0, which is OR.
The select lines 10 form the binary number 2, so the MUX routes input I₂ to the output.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A Mealy machine can respond to an input within the same clock cycle.  Reason (R): Its outputs depend directly on the present input as well as the state.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both statements are true. In a Mealy machine the output is a function of both state and current input, so a change at the input can change the output straight away, within the same clock cycle. So R explains A.
The minterms 5, 7, 13, 15 are 0101, 0111, 1101, 1111. B = 1 and D = 1 in all of them while A and C change, so the 4-cell group simplifies to BD.
11111100 is −4 in two's complement and 00000101 is +5. Their sum is −4 + 5 = 1 = 00000001, with no overflow because the operands have opposite signs.
Chips needed = (4K×8)/(1K×4) = 4 (depth) × 2 (width) = 8. Two chips give an 8-bit word and four such pairs give 4K locations.

questions.q: f_max with t_cq 2 ns, logic 15 ns, t_su 3 ns
questions.why: The minimum clock period is t_cq + logic + t_su = 2 + 15 + 3 = 20 ns, so f_max = 1/20 ns = 50 MHz.

questions.q: 10-bit ADC, 5 V full scale: code for 2.5 V (V/q, q = 5/1024)
questions.why: Step q = 5/1024 ≈ 0.00488 V. The code for 2.5 V is 2.5/0.00488 = 512, which is exactly half of the 1024 codes.

questions.q: Case: A keypad sends codes when several keys are pressed together. Best encoder
questions.why: A priority encoder gives a valid code even when several inputs are active by choosing the highest-priority one. A simple encoder gives wrong outputs for multiple active inputs.

questions.q: Synchronous mod-8 up counter with JK: J₂ = K₂ =
questions.why: In a synchronous counter, a bit toggles only when all lower bits are 1. So the most significant flip-flop has J₂ = K₂ = Q₁Q₀ (toggle when both lower bits are 1).
An 8:1 MUX tree uses 4 MUXes in the first stage, 2 in the second and 1 in the last: 4 + 2 + 1 = 7 MUXes of 2:1.

questions.q: Fan-out: I_OL 20 mA / I_IL 0.5 mA; I_OH 1 mA / I_IH 50 µA
questions.why: Fan-out is the smaller of the two limits. Low state: 20/0.5 = 40. High state: 1 mA/50 µA = 20. The smaller one limits the gate, so fan-out = 20.
Ideal SNR = 6.02N + 1.76 dB. For N = 10: 60.2 + 1.76 ≈ 62 dB. The 74 dB figure belongs to a 12-bit ADC.

questions.q: Hazard-free SOP for F = A′C′ + AB
questions.why: F = A′C′ + AB has a hazard when A changes with B = 1 and C = 0. Adding the consensus term BC′ covers that transition, giving A′C′ + AB + BC′ without changing the function.
